You explicitly tag candidate prims with instanceable = true, and OpenUSD derives the prototypes implicitly from the authored composition arcs
You explicitly list each instance path, and OpenUSD implicitly disables overrides on the whole stage
explanation: The lesson states: "You tell OpenUSD the candidates for instancing, it figures out the prototypes implicitly from the authored composition arcs." Setting instanceable = true is the explicit signal; here the shared reference to RobotArm.usd yields one implicit prototype with two instances.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Scenegraph Instancing

stem: A TD authors an override on a prim shown in usdview as "/__Prototype_01" because it appeared editable in the tree view. Why is this override invalid?
choices: The override targets the prototype's runtime name, which composes more weakly than the instanceable prim's own opinions
The override targets a runtime data model that is not editable, producing a dangling opinion unrelated to the real prototype
The override must instead pass through the instanceable prim's xformOp attributes, the editable entry point to a prototype
The override authors primvars:asset_color as an array, while constant-interpolation primvars take a single tuple value
explanation: Prototype names like /__Prototype_01 are a runtime data model shown for inspection only; they are not editable, so the authored over is a dangling opinion unrelated to the actual prototype. The failure is not a composition-strength contest, xformOps on the instanceable prim govern transforms rather than serving as a general edit channel into prototypes, and the array form of the primvar value is not what invalidates the edit.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Scenegraph Instance Refinement

stem: Which scenegraph instance refinement techniques result in a NEW prototype being created?
choices: Authoring a unique xformOp:translate on the instanceable prim
Hierarchical refinement using primvars authored on the instanceable prim
Variant set refinement (selecting a different variant on the instanceable prim)
Ad hoc arcs refinement (adding a new composition arc to the instanceable prim)
explanation: Refinements that change an instance's composition trigger a new prototype. Variant selections are evaluated when OpenUSD determines implicit prototypes (new prototype), and adding an ad hoc composition arc creates a new prototype shared by instances with that arc. Primvar (hierarchical) refinement and per-instance transforms are natively inherited by the instanceable prim and create no new prototype.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Scenegraph Instance Refinement

stem: You must apply the same override to every instance in a group at once, keeping instancing enabled and authoring only a single opinion. Which refinement technique is intended for this case?
choices: Broadcasted refinement, authoring one opinion on a shared inherit or specialize target the instances point to
Hierarchical refinement, authoring an inherited primvar opinion on each instance's instanceable prim
Prototype refinement, authoring the shared opinion directly on the runtime prototype prim all instances use
Deinstancing refinement, authoring the opinion on each prim after setting instanceable to false across the group
explanation: Inherit and specialize arcs broadcast: a single opinion authored on the shared target namespace ripples to every instance that targets it, keeping instancing enabled. Hierarchical primvar refinement requires touching every instanceable prim rather than authoring once, runtime prototypes are not editable so authoring on them produces a dangling opinion, and deinstancing the group disables instancing and multiplies the authored edits.

stem: Several instances share one prototype, and some are given different colors via primvars authored on their instanceable prims. Why does this add shading variety without creating any new prototypes?
choices: Primvars are copied into each instance's prototype, so every colored instance quietly receives a private prototype
Primvars override the prototype's geometry opinions, so the differently colored instances merge into a single prototype
Primvars force OpenUSD to deinstance the prim before applying the value, so the prototype count stays unchanged
Primvars inherit down namespace, so the new opinion lives only on the instanceable prim and the instance subgraphs stay identical
explanation: Primvars inherit down the prim hierarchy, so the only new opinion sits on the instanceable prim while the subgraphs remain identical, and identical subgraphs mean no new prototype is needed. Prototypes are not copied per instance, primvar opinions do not modify the prototype's geometry or merge instances, and no deinstancing occurs when a primvar is authored.

stem: In a fully instanced scene, only one instance needs arbitrary overrides authored on its interior geometry. Which refinement technique is the simplest?
choices: Author the overrides directly on the instance proxy paths beneath the instanceable prim
Set instanceable = false on that prim in a stronger layer, then author the overrides on its subgraph
Author the overrides on a shared specialize target so they broadcast into the instance's subgraph
Add an ad hoc internal reference to the prim so the overrides compose into a new prototype
explanation: Deinstancing is the simplest refinement for one-off arbitrary edits: disabling instancing on that single prim in a stronger layer makes its whole subgraph editable. Instance proxies are read-only so direct authoring fails, broadcasting through a specialize target would affect every instance sharing the arc rather than one, and an ad hoc arc that spawns a new prototype is more machinery than a single uniquely edited copy needs.

stem: A PointInstancer must animate a subset of instances on and off over time, and separately must permanently prune others. Which property drives each, and what extra capability does the pruning property have?
choices: Use inactiveIds for animated on/off visibility; use invisibleIds to prune, and invisibleIds can be list-edited to sparsely add and remove ids
Use protoIndices for animated on/off visibility; use ids to prune, and ids can be list-edited to sparsely add and remove entries
Use ids for animated on/off visibility; use positions to prune, and positions can be list-edited to sparsely add and remove entries
Use invisibleIds for animated on/off visibility; use inactiveIds to prune, and inactiveIds can be list-edited to sparsely add and remove ids
explanation: The rule of thumb is invisibleIds for animating instances on and off over time and inactiveIds for pruning, and inactiveIds has the extra feature of being list-editable so ids can be sparsely added and removed. The first option swaps the two properties' roles, protoIndices selects prototypes rather than visibility, and ids and positions identify and place instances rather than hiding or pruning them.

stem: Why is it discouraged to instance a leaf gprim (e.g. a Mesh) directly, and what is the workaround if you want gprim-level instancing?
choices: Instanced gprims duplicate their vertex data per instance; mark the gprim with kind = component so the prototype is shared
Gprims cannot be targeted by reference arcs; convert the Mesh into a PointInstancer prototype and instance it by index
The root prim of an instance prototype has no properties, making direct gprim instancing pointless; add an Xform parent and reference the parent
Gprims may be instanced once protoIndices are authored on them; add the index array to the Mesh and reference it directly
explanation: Prototype root prims possess no properties, so instancing a gprim directly is pointless; the workaround is to add an Xform parent over the gprim in the prototype and have instances reference the parent. Instancing shares rather than duplicates prototype data, gprims are perfectly valid reference targets, and protoIndices belongs to PointInstancer and has no role in scenegraph instancing a Mesh.

stem: An asset's root layer is the primary means downstream users interact with it. Which metadata typically designates the single entry point prim that referencing will respect?
choices: The root layer's defaultPrim metadata
The upAxis metadata in the layer header
An instanceable = true tag on the World prim
The kind = component metadata on the deepest gprim
explanation: Most assets are organized around defined entry-point prims that act as the interface. A single asset entry point can typically be specified using the root layer's defaultPrim metadata, which OpenUSD's composition engine respects when referencing. Library assets with many entry points may instead organize them under scope prims.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is an Asset Interface?

stem: After referencing a building asset into a scene, the roof's material binding is dropped and OpenUSD warns that a relationship target "refers to a path outside the scope of the reference." What principle was violated and how is it fixed?
choices: Legibility: the material prim's name does not follow the asset's naming conventions, so re-author the binding with a conforming material name
Modularity: the binding crosses an asset boundary, so retarget it through an absolute path into a shared material library layer
Performance: the material loads with the heavy contents, so payload it to defer the binding until the reference is resolved
Encapsulation: relationship targets must be descendants of the asset's entry point; reparent the roof material under the entry point so it is encapsulated
explanation: Encapsulation requires that everything belonging to the asset, including relationship targets like bound materials, live as descendants of the entry-point prim; only prims beneath the entry point are brought over by a reference, so the fix is to reparent the roof material under it. Naming conventions (legibility) have no bearing on whether a target path survives referencing. Absolute paths into external layers make the cross-scope problem worse, not better. And payloading the material changes when it loads, not whether its path is inside the reference's scope.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Encapsulating Your Asset

stem: In the reference/payload pattern, a class and a variant set are lofted from the contents layer up to the interface layer, above the payload. Why are these inexpensive fields lofted?
choices: So that selecting a variant triggers the payload to load with the matching contents composed
So that the variant sets remain valid, since variant sets authored inside a payloaded layer are ignored
So that the payload arc behaves as a reference arc, composing the variant opinions eagerly
So the fields stay discoverable and usable while the payload is unloaded, avoiding payload loads in some contexts
explanation: Lofting moves important, inexpensive fields like variant sets and classes above the payload so they remain discoverable and usable while the payload is unloaded, which can avoid loading the payload at all in some contexts. Selecting a variant does not trigger payload loading; load state is controlled independently. Variant sets inside a payloaded layer are not ignored; the lofted set merely advertises the underlying one. And lofting does not change the payload arc into a reference or alter its deferred-loading behavior.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Reference/Payload Pattern?

stem: An asset offers two parameterization methods on its entry point: variant sets and primvars. With respect to scenegraph instancing, how do they differ?
choices: Both are compatible with instancing, and neither variant selections nor primvars generate new prototypes
Both are compatible with instancing, but primvar differences generate new prototypes, while variant selections do not
Both are compatible with instancing, but variant-selection differences generate new prototypes, while primvars do not
Both are compatible with instancing, and both variant-selection and primvar differences generate new prototypes
explanation: Both variant selections and primvars on an asset entry point are compatible with scenegraph instancing, but they differ in prototype cost: differing variant selections generate new prototypes for downstream contexts, while differing primvars do not, making primvars the lighter parameterization. The other combinations are wrong: it is false that neither generates prototypes, false that both do, and the claim that primvars generate prototypes while variants do not inverts the documented behavior.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Asset Parameterization?

stem: A studio splits an asset into separate geometry and shading layers combined in a layer stack to model workstreams. Which statements are correct guidance?
choices: Parallel workstream layers let a modeler and a surfacer iterate independently, each authoring its contributions sparsely
Workstream layers should be merged into a single layer at publish time so consumers resolve a deterministic result
Each workstream layer should re-author the other workstreams' opinions so the composed result is self-contained
Layer stacks are not a replacement for asset versioning systems, and workstreams that grow procedurally over time should be avoided
explanation: Splitting geometry and shading into parallel workstream layers lets artists iterate independently, with each workstream ideally authoring only its unique contributions sparsely; and layer stacks are explicitly not a replacement for asset versioning systems, with procedurally growing workstreams to be avoided because each layer carries a resolve-and-open cost. Merging everything into one layer at publish defeats the layered workflow and is not the recommended guidance. Re-authoring other workstreams' opinions is the opposite of sparse authoring and needlessly overwrites their work.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Modeling Workstreams With Layer Stacks

stem: Reviewing this layer for model hierarchy validity, the Cube "Body" is a leaf gprim under a component. Which prim, if tagged kind = component, would make this model hierarchy invalid?
choices: Tagging "Component" with kind = component, because component models require an assembly parent rather than a group
Tagging "World" with kind = group, because the ancestors of a component model may not carry the group kind
Leaving "Body" untagged, because every descendant of a component model must carry the subcomponent kind
Tagging "Body" with kind = component, because a component is a leaf model that cannot appear beneath another component model
explanation: component denotes a leaf model and pruning point, so component models cannot contain other component models as descendants; tagging the Cube "Body" (which sits beneath the component "Component") with kind = component would make the hierarchy invalid. The other changes are all legal: "Component" already validly carries component under a group ancestor, since ancestors must be group or a subkind of group such as assembly (not assembly specifically, and group is required rather than forbidden), and descendants of a component are expected to be untagged because they sit below the pruning boundary.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Are Model Kinds?

stem: The model hierarchy is designed to be shallow. What is the cited reason and what is the explicit sign that a hierarchy is too "deep"?
choices: Shallow hierarchies reduce draw calls because Hydra batches prims by model kind; a Scope prim holding materials is the sign that a hierarchy is deep
kind metadata is consulted at render time rather than during composition, so depth carries no composition cost; a subcomponent tag is the sign that a hierarchy is deep
kind metadata is read during composition for all model-hierarchy members, so a shallow structure minimizes that cost; a gprim tagged as a component is the sign that a hierarchy is deep
Shallow hierarchies keep prim paths short, which speeds path resolution; a payload authored beneath a component is the sign that a hierarchy is deep
explanation: kind metadata is explicitly read during composition for all members of the model hierarchy, so costs are minimized in a shallow structure, and a gprim tagged as a component is the explicit sign that a hierarchy is deep. The cited reason is composition cost, not Hydra draw-call batching or prim-path resolution speed, and neither a material-holding Scope nor a payload beneath a component is the documented depth indicator. The render-time claim is backwards, since kind is consulted during composition, and a subcomponent tag is a normal intra-model marker, not the depth sign.

stem: A point instance that fell out of a box during simulation must be replaced with a fully editable, animatable character asset at the exact same location. Which described workflow accomplishes this "promotion"?
choices: Set the instance's entry in protoIndices to a new prototype index, then add the character asset to the prototypes relationship
Deactivate the instance via inactiveIds, then reference the new asset and place it with the transform from ComputeInstanceTransformsAtTime() for that id
Author an override on that instance's element of the positions array, then parent the character asset under the PointInstancer's prototype root
Add the instance's id to invisibleIds, then reference the new asset and place it using the prototype's root transform
explanation: Promotion deactivates the point instance with inactiveIds, then references the editable character asset and positions it using ComputeInstanceTransformsAtTime(), which combines the prototype root transform with the instance-specific transform. Swapping the protoIndices entry only points the instance at a different prototype; it remains a non-editable point instance. Per-element sparse overrides of the positions array are not supported, and parenting the character under the prototype root would affect every instance of that prototype. invisibleIds is for animating instances on and off rather than permanent replacement, and the prototype's root transform alone omits the instance-specific transform needed for exact placement.

stem: OpenUSD recently introduced a new composition arc that added a letter to the strength-ordering acronym, turning LIVRPS into LIVERPS. What is this arc and where does it sit in the strength ordering?
choices: Relocates; it is the 'E' (rElocates) and sits between variant sets and references in the ordering
Relocates; it is the 'E' (rElocates) and sits ahead of local opinions as the strongest arc
Specializes; the 'E' marks an 'extends' arc that becomes the new weakest arc below specializes
References; the 'E' distinguishes external references, which sit between inherits and variant sets
explanation: The new arc is relocates, represented by the 'E' (rElocates) in LIVERPS: Local, Inherits, VariantSets, rElocates, References, Payloads, Specializes, so it sits between variant sets and references. It is not the strongest arc, since local opinions remain strongest. The 'E' is not an 'extends' arc below specializes, which remains the weakest arc. And it has nothing to do with external references, which do not move between inherits and variant sets or change the acronym.

stem: What does the relocates composition arc do, and what constraint applies to the paths it uses?
choices: It copies attribute time samples from a source prim to a target prim, using mappings that may name either prim paths or property paths
It removes the source prim from the referenced layer and reauthors it at the target path, permanently rewriting the composition source
It is authored on the prim itself like a reference, and its mappings may remap both prim paths and individual property paths
It non-destructively renames or reparents a prim brought in across a composition arc, using layer-metadata source-to-target mappings that may be prim paths only, not property paths
explanation: Relocates non-destructively maps a prim path from a remote layer stack to a new path in the local namespace, authored as source-to-target mappings in layer metadata, and those paths can only be prim paths, not property paths. It does not copy time samples between prims, and property paths are never valid in the mapping. It does not remove or rewrite the composition source, because the operation is non-destructive. And it lives in layer metadata, not on the prim the way a reference is authored.

stem: A layer prepends a reference in a WEAK sublayer and appends a reference of the same type in a STRONGER sublayer onto the same prim. Which statements about list-editing resolution are correct?
choices: Reset-to-explicit (e.g. references = @file.usd@) merges the explicit list with list ops contributed by weaker layers
Attributes participate in this same list editing, so attribute values can also be prepended and appended
An appended arc is placed at the back of the resolved list and is therefore weaker than arcs prepended from weaker layers
A prepended arc in a weaker layer is still stronger than any same-type arc that is appended from stronger layers
The appended arc resolves stronger than the prepend because it was authored in the stronger layer
explanation: Appended arcs go to the back of the resolved list, so a prepended arc, even one authored in a weaker layer, is stronger than same-type arcs appended from stronger layers; here the weak-layer prepend wins. The claim that the append resolves stronger because its layer is stronger reverses that rule. Reset-to-explicit does not merge with weaker layers' list ops; it ignores them and resets the list outright. And attributes can never be list edited, so attribute values cannot be prepended or appended.

stem: Which of the following USD data elements are list editable across composition arcs?
choices: SubLayer lists authored in a layer's metadata
Attribute values such as a float radius on a prim
Relationships and their targets
Integer and string/token array custom metadata
References, inherits, specializes, and variant sets
explanation: List-editable elements include relationships, references, inherits, specializes, variant sets, and integer and string/token array custom metadata. Attribute values are never list editable, because list editing time-varying values would be prohibitively expensive. And subLayer lists are the one composition mechanism excluded from list editing.

stem: When the LIVERPS algorithm recurses into a targeted layer stack while resolving inherits, variant sets, references, or payloads, what special treatment does the specializes ('S') step receive?
choices: Specializes is evaluated twice within each recursion so its fallback opinions can win over those of references and payloads
Specializes is no longer evaluated during composition because the relocates arc replaced it in the current strength ordering
Specializes is evaluated first inside every recursion, making it effectively the strongest arc within referenced layer stacks
Specializes is skipped while recursing into the other arcs; full LIVERPS including the S step is re-applied only when resolving specializes targets
explanation: While recursing into the layer stacks targeted by inherits, variants, relocates, references, and payloads, the algorithm ignores specializes arcs; the full LIVERPS evaluation, including the S step, is re-applied only when resolving specializes targets themselves. This is what keeps specializes the weakest, fallback arc. It is not evaluated twice so its fallback can beat references and payloads, it is not evaluated first inside recursions as a strongest arc, and it was not replaced by relocates, which was added elsewhere in the ordering.

stem: Layer A references layer B with a time-scale of 2.0, and layer B references layer C with a time-scale of 3.5. When data whose source is C is resolved at A, what total time-scale is applied?
choices: 7.0, because layer offsets compose by multiplying through the chain of arcs
2.0, because the outermost offset on the strongest arc supersedes deeper offsets
5.5, because layer offsets compose by adding the scales together
3.5, because the offset nearest the data source supersedes outer offsets
explanation: Layer offsets compose multiplicatively through the chain of arcs, so resolving at A applies both offsets and yields 2.0 x 3.5 = 7.0 for content authored in the deepest referenced layer. The scales are not added together to give 5.5. And no single offset supersedes the others: neither the outermost offset on the stronger arc nor the offset nearest the data source applies alone, because every offset along the chain participates.

stem: Given the root layer below, sublayer1.usda itself sublayers sublayer1A.usda then sublayer1B.usda. In the resolved local strength order, how do opinions in sublayer1B.usda compare to those in sublayer2.usda?

snippets.code:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./sublayer1.usda@,
        @./sublayer2.usda@
    ]
)

choices: They are equal in strength, because every layer in a single layer stack contributes opinions at one shared priority level
sublayer2.usda is stronger, because nested sublayers are consulted after the top-level entries of the root layer stack
sublayer1B.usda is stronger, because sublayers are gathered depth-first and it belongs to the higher-listed sublayer1.usda
sublayer2.usda is stronger, because sublayers listed later in the root layer override those listed earlier
explanation: Sublayers are gathered recursively in depth-first order, so the sublayers of sublayer1.usda, including sublayer1B.usda, are stronger than sublayer2.usda because sublayer1.usda is listed higher. Layers in a stack are not all at one shared priority level; the gathered order defines strength. Nested sublayers are not consulted after all top-level entries, since depth-first gathering keeps them under their parent's position. And earlier-listed sublayers are stronger, so later-listed ones do not override them.

stem: A class prim supplies a maxspeed fallback of 30 via a specializes arc. Side streets are then authored directly to 20, and later the class fallback is changed to 40. What maxspeed do the side streets and main streets resolve to?
choices: Both side streets and main streets become 40, because the updated fallback is broadcast to each prim that specializes the class
Side streets and main streets revert to the schema default, because the directly authored opinions conflict with the updated fallback
Side streets become 40 and main streets stay at 30, because the new fallback reaches refined prims while unrefined prims keep their first value
Main streets pick up 40 from the new fallback, but side streets stay at 20 because their directly authored opinion is stronger than the specializes fallback
explanation: Specializes supplies fallback values, so the unrefined main streets adopt the new fallback of 40 while the side streets keep their directly authored 20, which is stronger than any specializes opinion. The broadcast does not reach prims that have their own authored opinion, so not every road becomes 40. Nothing reverts to a schema default, because strength ordering resolves the difference rather than treating it as a conflict. And the direction is not reversed: refined prims ignore the new fallback while unrefined prims take it.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Experimenting With Specializes

stem: An inherit arc targets an unencapsulated class outside the referenced prim's hierarchy. When the asset is referenced elsewhere and that class is overridden, what is the effect, and what is this pattern called?
choices: Global refinement: the unencapsulated class path is not re-pathed on reference, so the override broadcasts to every prim that inherits it
Destructive edit: the override is written back into the asset's source layer, so the original file on disk carries the new opinions
Local refinement: the class path is re-pathed per reference, so the override affects only one referenced instance
Broken arc: the inherit target fails to resolve once the asset is referenced, because the class lies outside the referenced hierarchy
explanation: This is global refinement: an inherit target outside encapsulation never gets re-pathed on reference, so overriding the class broadcasts to every prim that inherits it within the referencing context. Local refinement is the opposite case, where an encapsulated target is re-pathed per reference and the override stays with one instance. The edit is non-destructive, landing in the stronger layer rather than the asset's source file. And the arc does not break, since unencapsulated inherit targets keep resolving after the asset is referenced, which is exactly what the pattern exploits.

stem: A prim references an asset using an inner Cube as the source prim, rather than the asset's root World prim. The Cube has a material binding to a material defined under World. What is the result?
choices: The Cube's geometry composes but the material binding is dropped with a warning, because the bound material lies outside the scope of the reference
Nothing composes onto the prim, because a reference whose source prim is not the layer's defaultPrim fails to resolve and is skipped
Both the Cube and its material compose, because relationship targets are re-pathed to follow their prim across the reference
The material composes but the geometry is dropped, because relationship targets take precedence over prim specs during grafting
explanation: A reference grafts only the targeted source prim's subtree, so targeting Cube brings the geometry but not the material defined under World; the binding's target falls outside the scope of the reference, and USD warns and ignores it. The reference still resolves even though Cube is not the defaultPrim, because an explicit prim path is supplied. Relationship targets are not re-pathed to chase out-of-scope prims, so the material does not follow the Cube across. And grafting never drops geometry in favor of a relationship target.

stem: Within a single variant set on a prim, which kinds of edits can the selected variant make to the prim and its descendants?
choices: Define new descendant prims and override their properties, but not author composition arcs inside the variant
Override attribute values on the prim and its descendants, but neither define new prims nor author composition arcs
Sparsely override properties, define new descendant prims, and author new composition arcs (such as a reference) that exist only within that variant
Edit metadata on the prim and its descendants, but leave property values and prim definitions to stronger layers
explanation: A selected variant can do all three documented things: sparsely override properties on the prim or any descendant, define new descendant prims (like the ExtraCube), and author new composition arcs such as a reference that exist only within that variant. Each narrower option is wrong because it denies one of these capabilities: variants are not barred from authoring composition arcs, not limited to overriding values without defining prims, and not restricted to metadata edits.

stem: A reference arc omits the asset/file identifier and supplies only a prim path, e.g. references = </Master>. How does USD interpret this, versus when both an asset path and prim path are given?
choices: Omitting the identifier produces a composition error when the stage opens; a reference must supply both an asset path and a prim path to resolve
Omitting the identifier turns the arc into an inherit targeting the named prim; supplying an asset path is what distinguishes references from inherits
Omitting the identifier converts the arc into a payload on the same prim; supplying an asset path keeps it an eagerly composed reference
Omitting the identifier makes it an internal reference targeting a prim in the same layer; supplying an asset path makes it an external reference grafting from another file
explanation: References can be external, targeting a prim in a different layer via an asset path, or internal, targeting a prim within the same layer when the identifier is omitted. An internal reference is valid, so no composition error occurs and both parts are not required. The arc remains a reference rather than becoming an inherit, and it does not become a payload, which is a separate arc with deferred loading regardless of whether an asset path is present.

stem: Why does UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack require a timeCode argument, and how should its result be used?
choices: With value clips, the set of layers contributing to an attribute can change over time, so the stack may need recomputation per frame
Its result should be used only for debugging and diagnostic purposes, not for value resolution
The returned property specs already carry the layer-offset-adjusted samples needed to retrieve correct animated values
Retaining the returned stack is faster than a UsdAttributeQuery for repeated value resolution, so it should replace that query
The timeCode is required because the prim index itself is rebuilt at each frame, so composition must be recomputed per timeCode
explanation: The timeCode argument is required because, in the presence of value clips, the set of layers contributing to an attribute can change over time, so the stack may need recomputation per frame; and the result is documented for debugging and diagnostics only, not for value resolution. The returned specs do not carry the layer-offset-adjusted samples needed for correct animated values when layer offsets are present, which is precisely why the stack cannot drive resolution. Retaining the stack is not a supported substitute for a UsdAttributeQuery, which is the documented way to speed repeated resolution. And the prim index is cached rather than rebuilt per frame, so composition is not recomputed at every timeCode.

stem: While debugging a prim, you want the list of PrimSpecs contributing to the prim's metadata, and separately the list of PropertySpecs contributing to one property's value. Which APIs return these two things?

snippets.code:
prim = stage.GetPrimAtPath('/Char')
prim_specs = prim.GetPrimStack()                     # PrimSpecs -> prim metadata
attr = prim.GetAttribute('displayColor')
prop_specs = attr.GetPropertyStack(Usd.TimeCode.Default())  # PropertySpecs

choices: UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack returns the PrimSpecs for the prim's metadata, and UsdPrim::GetPrimStack returns the PropertySpecs for the property's value
UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack returns both the PrimSpecs and the PropertySpecs, recorded on each contributing site it visits
UsdPrim::GetPrimStack returns both the PrimSpecs and the PropertySpecs, since a property stack is a filtered view of the prim stack
UsdPrim::GetPrimStack returns the PrimSpecs for the prim's metadata, and UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack returns the PropertySpecs for the property's value
explanation: UsdPrim::GetPrimStack returns the prim specs contributing opinions to a composed prim's metadata, while UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack returns the property specs contributing a property's value; they are distinct APIs at different namespace levels. The assignment that puts the PrimSpecs on GetPropertyStack and the PropertySpecs on GetPrimStack is exactly reversed. Neither API returns both lists: the property specs returned by GetPropertyStack do not bundle the prim-level specs, and a property stack is not a filtered view of the prim stack.

stem: An EditTarget is used to direct authored opinions to a specific contributing site. Which sites can a UsdEditTarget select?

snippets.code:
stage.SetEditTarget(Usd.EditTarget(sublayer))
# or scope edits to a variant:
with vset.GetVariantEditContext():
    prim.GetAttribute('color').Set((1,0,0))

choices: Any sublayer in the stage's root layer stack, the currently selected variant of a defined variant set, or any node in a prim's index such as a reference target
Any sublayer in the stage's root layer stack or the session layer, with variant edits authored by opening the variant's source layer as its own stage
The currently selected variant of a defined variant set or the session layer, with sublayer edits authored by opening the sublayer as its own stage
Any reference or payload target in a prim's index, with local sublayer and variant edits routed through the stage's root layer
explanation: A UsdEditTarget can select any sublayer in the stage's root layer stack, the currently selected variant of any defined variant set, or any node in a prim's index, which allows targeting inherited classes, reference targets, and similar sites. Variant edits do not require opening the variant's source layer as its own stage, because variants are directly selectable through the edit target. Sublayer edits likewise do not require opening the sublayer as a separate stage, because sublayers are directly selectable. And local sublayer and variant edits are not routed through the root layer; the edit target addresses each contributing site directly.

stem: A pipeline tool authors animated overrides into a 'clip' USD layer that is composed onto the stage via value clips, but a reference authored inside that clip file is being ignored. Why?
choices: The stage ignores composition arcs contained in a clip layer, so value clips can usefully contain only direct local opinions on the attributes they modify
The reference inside the clip is composed, but its opinions lose to the clip's stronger time samples under LIVERPS strength ordering
Arcs inside a clip layer are honored only when the clip set declares a manifest, so the missing clip manifest causes the reference to be dropped
Value clips mute every reference arc across the stage while the clip set is active, not just the arcs inside the clip file
explanation: For performance and scalability reasons, a UsdStage ignores any composition arcs contained in a clip USD file, which means value clips can only usefully contain direct local opinions about the attributes they modify. The reference is never composed at all, so this is not a case of composed opinions losing to clip time samples under LIVERPS. A clip manifest declares which attributes the clips provide; it does not enable arcs inside clip layers, so its absence is not the cause. And nothing is muted stage-wide: reference arcs outside the clip files continue to compose normally.

stem: A teammate claims composition results are cached but value resolution is not. Which statements from the USD value-resolution model are correct?
choices: GetPropertyStack should be used as the primary value-resolution path for performance
Composition (the prim index) is cached for fast access; the USD core does not pre-compute or cache per-composed-property values
To speed up repeated value queries on an attribute, a client can construct and retain a UsdAttributeQuery or UsdResolveInfo
How data combines during value resolution is identical for every metadatum, regardless of its data type
Value resolution is internally multi-threaded by USD, so opening many stages in parallel threads is the recommended way to scale
explanation: Composition is cached as a prim-level index for fast access, while the USD core does not pre-compute or cache per-composed-property values, and clients can construct and retain a UsdAttributeQuery or UsdResolveInfo to speed repeated queries on an attribute. GetPropertyStack is documented for debugging only, not as a resolution path. How data combines during value resolution is specific to each metadatum and varies by data type — dictionaries, for example, merge element by element — so it is not identical across metadata. And it is composition that is internally multi-threaded; value resolution is designed to be efficiently multi-threaded by clients, not scaled by opening many stages in parallel.

stem: After referencing an asset, a material binding stops working and USD warns that a relationship target 'refers to a path outside the scope of the reference ... Ignoring.' What is the most likely root cause and fix?
choices: The binding uses bindMaterialAs weakerThanDescendants, so a descendant's binding wins after composition; strengthening the binding on the referencing side restores it
The reference maps the asset's default prim, but the bound material sits under a deactivated ancestor; reactivating that ancestor restores the target
The relationship target was authored as a relative path that re-resolved against the wrong prim; converting the target to an absolute stage path repairs the binding
The bound material was not encapsulated under the referenced source prim; re-author the asset so dependent prims such as the material live under the default prim
explanation: The warning means the binding relationship targets a path outside the scope of the referenced prim: the material was not encapsulated under the referenced source prim, so the fix is to re-author the asset so all dependent prims, including the material, live under the default prim being referenced. The bindMaterialAs strength setting governs conflicts with descendant bindings and would not produce an out-of-scope warning. A deactivated ancestor would prune the material from composition, but the warning explicitly cites a path outside the reference's scope, not an inactive prim. And switching to an absolute stage path does not help, because any target outside the referenced hierarchy is ignored regardless of how the path is authored.

stem: OpenUSD's data exchange approach is loosely inspired by Extract-Transform-Load (ETL). How many phases does it have, and what are they?
choices: One phase: a single combined extract-and-transform conversion
Four phases: extract, transform, validate, then load
Three phases: extract, transform, then validate
Two phases: extract, then an optional transform
explanation: The data exchange approach has two phases: extract and transform. Extraction translates the data to OpenUSD as directly as possible to maintain fidelity to the source, and the transform phase consists of one or more optional steps added to better meet end-client needs. Validation (usdchecker) is a separate testing activity, not a third phase of the approach, and there is no load phase.

stem: In a DCC application's File > Import and File > Export menus, how are importers and exporters defined?
choices: Importers translate data from OpenUSD to the application's runtime format; exporters translate from the runtime format to OpenUSD
Both importers and exporters always translate bidirectionally between OpenUSD and the runtime format
Importers translate data from the runtime format to OpenUSD; exporters translate from OpenUSD to the runtime format
Importers convert USDA to USDC; exporters convert USDC to USDZ
explanation: Importers translate data from OpenUSD into the application's runtime format, and exporters translate from the application's runtime format to OpenUSD. They are implemented as part of a DCC application and have a clear translation directionality, unlike standalone converters which may be one-way or two-way. The format-pair answer describes usdcat conversions, not import/export.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Exchange?

stem: Which statements about File Format Plugins, the OpenUSD-unique integration mechanism, are accurate?
choices: They translate in one direction, reading from the source file format without writing USD edits back to it
They can be bidirectional, both reading from and writing to the source format, and can compose non-file sources like databases
A stage can include a source format directly as a reference, payload, or sublayer, translated on the fly as it is read
They require the source file to be converted into a USDZ package before it can be composed onto a stage
They bake the source data into a static USD layer at import so the source file is no longer consulted
explanation: File format plugins can be bidirectional, supporting both reading and writing of the source format, and they can compose non-file-based sources such as databases or procedural content; a stage can include the source format directly as a reference, payload, or sublayer, translated on the fly while read as a layer. They are not restricted to one-way reading, no USDZ conversion is required, and baking into a static layer describes DCC importers/exporters, not plugins.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Exchange?

stem: A DCC tool exports OpenUSD that must later be reimported (round-trip) into the same tool. Which guidance preserves fidelity, and what work belongs in the transform phase?
choices: Apply as many transformations as possible during extraction so the source structure is discarded early
Perform all transformations inside the extraction function to guarantee a lossless round-trip
Treat export options, content re-structuring, and optimizations like mesh merging as transform-phase work
Store every transformation as a separate USDZ package to make round-trips reversible
Minimize data transformations, because extensive transformations complicate accurately reversing changes on reimport
explanation: For round-trip workflows you should minimize data transformations, because extensive transformations complicate reversing changes on reimport and risk information loss. The transform phase is where export options, content re-structuring, and optimizations such as mesh merging belong. Extraction should map the source as directly as possible (not discard it), transformations are kept out of extraction, and USDZ packaging is unrelated to round-trip reversibility.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Transformation?

stem: An obj2usd converter reads an OBJ material that supplies a SHININESS value, but UsdPreviewSurface expects roughness. How is the value mapped, and which workflow flag is set?

snippets.code:
roughness = 1 - math.sqrt(mtl["SHININESS"] / 1000.0)
shader.CreateInput("useSpecularWorkflow", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Int).Set(1)
shader.CreateInput("roughness", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(roughness)

choices: Author the raw shininess value directly on a shininess input and leave useSpecularWorkflow unset
Copy shininess into the roughness input unchanged because the two are equivalent
Set roughness equal to shininess / 1000.0 directly and enable the metallic PBR workflow
Convert shininess to roughness with roughness = 1 - sqrt(shininess / 1000.0) and set useSpecularWorkflow to 1
explanation: The converter derives roughness from the OBJ shininess using roughness = 1 - sqrt(shininess / 1000.0) and sets useSpecularWorkflow to 1, because the specular workflow maps most directly to the data coming from OBJ. UsdPreviewSurface has no raw shininess input, the values are not equivalent, and a metallic/PBR workflow is not the directly-mapped choice here.

stem: Which Python sequence creates a shader, identifies it as UsdPreviewSurface, and connects it as the material's surface output to produce the material shown below?
choices: Define a UsdGeom.Shader, call CreateTypeAttr('UsdPreviewSurface'), then connect it with material.CreateSurfaceOutput().ConnectToSource(shader.GetPath())
Define a UsdShade.Shader, call CreateIdAttr('UsdPreviewSurface'), then material.CreateSurfaceOutput().ConnectToSource(shader.ConnectableAPI(), UsdShade.Tokens.surface)
Define a UsdShade.Shader, set a 'surface' string attribute on the Material prim naming the shader's path, then apply MaterialBindingAPI to the Material
Define the shader under a UsdShade.NodeGraph, call CreateIdAttr('UsdPreviewSurface'), then let namespace proximity connect outputs:surface to the Material
explanation: The graph is built by defining a UsdShade.Shader, identifying it with CreateIdAttr('UsdPreviewSurface'), and connecting the material's surface output to the shader via material.CreateSurfaceOutput().ConnectToSource(shader.ConnectableAPI(), UsdShade.Tokens.surface). Shaders live in UsdShade rather than UsdGeom and their id is set with CreateIdAttr not a type attribute, the connection is an explicit output connection rather than a string attribute plus binding schema, and outputs are never connected by namespace proximity.

stem: OBJ has no scene-graph root, so a freshly extracted stage has multiple prims under the pseudo-root and no defaultPrim. Which transform-phase step produces the referenceable result shown below?
choices: Flatten the stage into a single layer so the pseudo-root's children collapse into one prim that becomes the defaultPrim
Package the stage as USDZ with usdzip, which assigns the first root prim as defaultPrim during packaging
Define a /World Xform, set it as defaultPrim, and reparent the root prims under it with Usd.NamespaceEditor
Set defaultPrim to one of the existing mesh prims and reference the remaining prims individually by path
explanation: The transform step defines a /World Xform, sets it as defaultPrim, and reparents the root-namespace prims under it with Usd.NamespaceEditor so the asset shares one ancestor and can be referenced as a unit. Flattening merges opinions but never collapses root prims into a common ancestor, USDZ packaging assigns no defaultPrim, and pointing defaultPrim at one mesh leaves the rest of the asset outside the referenced hierarchy.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Transforming the Prim Hierarchy

stem: An obj2usd converter has an optional --up-axis export option. OBJ is Y-up, but the target pipeline is Z-up. Beyond writing the upAxis metadata, what does the converter do to produce the result shown below, and why?
choices: It rewrites each mesh's points attribute, swapping the Y and Z coordinates so the geometry is encoded natively Z-up
It authors the upAxis token alone, since Hydra reorients Y-up content when the stage metadata changes
It adds a +90-degree rotate-X op suffixed 'unitsResolve' on the defaultPrim, reorienting the content upright in the new system
It re-runs the extraction phase with a Z-up import flag so the vertices arrive pre-rotated from the source
explanation: The converter applies a corrective +90-degree rotateX op, suffixed 'unitsResolve' by convention, on the defaultPrim so the Y-up content remains upright in the Z-up stage. Vertex data is not rewritten, the runtime does not reorient content from metadata alone, and the correction is a transform-phase op rather than a re-extraction with different import settings.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Adding an Export Option

stem: While fixing usdchecker errors in an obj2usd converter, you need to author the stage's upAxis and linear-unit metadata. In which OpenUSD module are these geometric stage-metadata APIs found, and what values fit OBJ?

snippets.code:
UsdGeom.SetStageUpAxis(stage, UsdGeom.Tokens.y)
UsdGeom.SetStageMetersPerUnit(stage, UsdGeom.LinearUnits.meters)

choices: UsdGeom; OBJ is Y-up so set upAxis to Y, and OBJ is unitless so leave metersPerUnit unset for usdchecker to infer
Usd.Stage; OBJ is Z-up so set upAxis to Z, and OBJ specifies centimeters so set metersPerUnit to 0.01
Sdf.Layer; OBJ is Y-up so set upAxis to Y, and the units are stored as custom layer metadata fields
UsdGeom; OBJ is Y-up so set upAxis to Y, and OBJ is unitless so meters is chosen as a sensible default
explanation: These geometric stage-metadata APIs live in UsdGeom rather than Usd.Stage; the OBJ spec defines Y as up, and because OBJ is unitless the converter picks meters as a sensible default via SetStageMetersPerUnit. Leaving metersPerUnit unset is exactly the error usdchecker flags and nothing infers it, OBJ is neither Z-up nor centimeter-based, and these values are first-class stage metadata, not custom Sdf.Layer fields.

stem: Your team wants a richer validation workflow than the usdchecker command line. What does the Omniverse Asset Validator add on top of usdchecker?
choices: A graphical user interface for asset validation
Automatic fixes for failed validations and the ability to add new rules
A packaging step that bundles validated assets into USDZ archives
A flattening step that bakes composed stages into single delivery layers
A conversion step that rewrites ASCII layers into Crate binary
explanation: The Omniverse Asset Validator is based on usdchecker and adds a user interface, a Python API, automatic fixes for failed validations, and the ability to add new rules. It performs no USDZ packaging (that is usdzip's job), no stage flattening, and no ASCII-to-Crate conversion (those are usdcat operations), so none of those are capabilities it adds.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Asset Validation?

stem: The output of the extraction phase is often transient data. What is the recommended practice for this transient extracted stage, and why?
choices: Flatten the extracted stage into the transformed stage, because keeping the two stages separate complicates delivery
Write only the transformed stage to disk, because the extracted form duplicates data already held in the source file
Discard the extracted stage once the transform completes, because retaining it risks exposing proprietary source data
Optionally expose the in-memory extracted stage or write it to disk, because third-party developers may build their own transformations on it
explanation: The recommendation is to optionally give access to the in-memory extracted stage or write it to disk, since it is valuable to third-party developers who want to author their own transformation steps instead of reverse-engineering yours. Flattening it into the transformed stage or withholding it removes that access, and the guidance treats sharing the extracted stage as desirable rather than a data-exposure risk.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Extraction?

stem: Why is producing a conceptual data mapping document recommended while building an extraction implementation?
choices: It compresses the extracted source assets into a single USDZ archive ready for downstream delivery
It makes the round-trip lossless by resolving each schema gap before extraction begins
It serves as a data specification for the extraction and lets stakeholders participate in setting requirements
It replaces usdchecker validation by documenting each rule the converted asset must satisfy
It enables community feedback and communicates schema gaps where a source data model has no USD equivalent
explanation: A conceptual data mapping document acts as the data specification for the extraction implementation, letting stakeholders help set requirements and expectations, and it enables discourse with the community while surfacing schema gaps where source concepts have no USD equivalent. Documenting a mapping cannot itself make a round-trip lossless or resolve gaps, it does not substitute for running usdchecker, and it has nothing to do with USDZ packaging.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Extraction?

stem: Which statement correctly describes the reusability difference between extraction code and transformation code across multiple exporters?
choices: Extraction code is largely unique per source format, while transformation code can be shared across exporters since it operates on OpenUSD data
Extraction code and transformation code are both unique per source format, since each exporter targets a different data model
Transformation code is unique to each source format, while extraction code is reusable since all sources parse into OpenUSD
Extraction code and transformation code are both reusable across source formats, since every exporter emits OpenUSD data
explanation: Extraction code from a source format to OpenUSD is largely unique, while export options, optimizations, and asset-structure transformation code can be shared across exporters because it all operates on OpenUSD data. The reversed claim swaps the two, and the all-unique and all-reusable variants each contradict half of the documented split.

stem: OBJ stores one global vertex list grouped per face, but UsdGeom.Mesh prefers a flattened index list recomposed via face vertex counts, as in the Mesh below. In a loop over each face's index group, how are faceVertexCounts and faceVertexIndices assembled?

snippets.code:
#usda 1.0

def Mesh "Cube"
{
    int[] faceVertexCounts = [4, 4, 4]
    int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 3, 5, 4]
    uniform token subdivisionScheme = "none"
}

choices: Extend faceVertexIndices with each face's indices to build one flat list, and append len(indices) per face to faceVertexCounts
Store the vertex coordinates in faceVertexIndices and the index numbers in faceVertexCounts
Append each face's index tuple as a nested list into faceVertexIndices and leave faceVertexCounts empty
Copy the OBJ global index list directly into faceVertexIndices unchanged with no per-face counts
explanation: USD prefers a flattened index list plus an ordered list of face vertex counts. The converter extends faceVertexIndices with each face's indices (flattening them into one continuous list) and appends len(indices) per face to faceVertexCounts, so the faces can be recomposed. USD does not accept nested per-face lists, the OBJ grouping must be flattened (not copied verbatim), and the two arrays hold indices and counts, not coordinates.

stem: A stage sets timeCodesPerSecond = 24 and an attribute has a time sample at time code 48.0. How many seconds of playback after time code 0 does this sample represent?
choices: 24.0 seconds
2.0 seconds
48.0 seconds
1.0 second
explanation: Time code ordinates are scaled to seconds by dividing by the root layer's timeCodesPerSecond metadata. With timeCodesPerSecond = 24, a time code of 48.0 corresponds to 48/24 = 2.0 seconds. Time codes themselves are unitless; the seconds mapping comes only from timeCodesPerSecond.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Time Codes and Time Samples

stem: A stage starts at time code 1, but an attribute's first authored time sample is at time code 60. What value does the attribute resolve to when queried at time code 1, before the first sample?
choices: (1.5, 1.5, 1.5) — the authored default value
An interpolated value between the default and the first sample
(0, 0, 0) — no value resolves before the first sample
(2.5, 2.5, 2.5) — the first (earliest) time sample, held/clamped
explanation: When a time before the first authored sample is queried, USD clamps to and returns the first (earliest) time sample value, (2.5, 2.5, 2.5) here. Because time samples exist, they win over the authored default during value resolution at a non-Default time code. The default (1.5,1.5,1.5) is only returned for Get(Usd.TimeCode.Default()).

stem: On an animated stage, an attribute has both an authored default and time samples. What does Get() with no time code return, and which call instead retrieves the first animated value?
choices: The interpolated value at the current frame is returned; Get(0) retrieves the default
The first time sample is returned; Get(Usd.TimeCode.Default()) retrieves the default
The default value is returned; Get(Usd.TimeCode.EarliestTime()) retrieves the first time sample
An error is raised because a time code is required when time samples exist
explanation: Get() with no time code is equivalent to Get(Usd.TimeCode.Default()), which returns the authored (non-time-varying) default, not the animation. To get the actual first animated value you use Get(Usd.TimeCode.EarliestTime()). This is a common pitfall on animated stages.

stem: Two sublayers each author customData on the same prim. The stronger layer sets keys 'source' and 'opinion'; the weaker sets 'source' and 'unique_layer_value'. Which rule produces the composed result below?
choices: Weakest-opinion-wins per key: shared keys keep the weaker layer's value, while keys unique to the stronger layer persist
Per-key resolution: shared key 'source' takes the stronger opinion, while keys unique to the weaker layer (unique_layer_value) persist
List-edit merging: values for shared keys are appended in strength order, producing one entry per contributing layer
Whole-value resolution: the strongest layer's entire dictionary wins, replacing the keys from weaker layers
explanation: Dictionary-valued metadata like customData resolves element by element: the shared key 'source' takes the stronger layer's opinion ('layer_2'), while 'unique_layer_value', authored only in the weaker layer, persists - matching the composed result shown. Weakest-opinion-wins per key would have produced source = 'layer_1'; list-edit appending would have produced multiple entries for 'source'; and whole-value replacement would have dropped 'unique_layer_value' entirely.

stem: Which statements about OpenUSD metadata are correct?
choices: Metadata can be authored on prims but not on properties, layers, or the stage
Metadata is non-animatable and cannot be stored as time samples
Metadata is part of the core schema and data model in the same way typed attributes are
Most metadata resolves strongest-opinion-wins, while dictionaries like customData merge per key
explanation: Metadata cannot be sampled over time, which lets it be evaluated and stored more efficiently than attribute values, and while most metadata resolves by strongest-opinion-wins, dictionary types such as customData combine element by element. The remaining statements are false: metadata can be authored on prims, properties, layers, and the stage, and metadata is explicitly separate from the core schema and data model rather than part of it like typed attributes.

stem: A 6-meter tree authored with metersPerUnit = 1.0 is referenced into a stage with metersPerUnit = 0.01, with no corrective transform. How does it compose into the scene?
choices: It fails to compose, because the referenced layer's metersPerUnit conflicts with the stage's
It composes at 6 meters tall, because USD automatically converts linear units during composition
It composes at 6 centimeters tall, because USD does not automatically reconcile metersPerUnit
It composes at 600 meters tall, because USD multiplies values by the inverse of the unit ratio
explanation: USD copies geometric values literally and does not automatically reconcile metersPerUnit, so the raw value 6 is read in the referencing stage's 0.01 m/unit metric: the tree composes 6 centimeters tall - 100 times too small - until the assembler applies a corrective transform. Composition does not fail on differing unit metadata, no automatic conversion keeps it at 6 meters, and no inverse-ratio upscaling to 600 meters occurs.

stem: A USD file does not explicitly author metersPerUnit or upAxis. According to OpenUSD's fallback behavior, how are these interpreted?
choices: metersPerUnit falls back to 0.01 (centimeters) and upAxis to Y
metersPerUnit falls back to 1.0 (meters) and upAxis to Z
Both fall back to undefined, raising an error on stage open
metersPerUnit falls back to 0.001 (millimeters) and upAxis to Y
explanation: When metersPerUnit is not authored, the fallback is 0.01 (centimeters). For upAxis, the fallback is 'Y'. Pipelines should not assume meters/Z-up unless they are explicitly authored.

stem: An asset animated at 60 fps (timeCodesPerSecond = 60) is referenced into a scene whose stage uses timeCodesPerSecond = 24. Unlike linear units, how does USD treat this timing difference during composition?
choices: It clamps the referenced animation to the scene's start and end time codes
It composes the time samples literally, so the referenced animation plays back 2.5x too fast
It skips composing the referenced animation, because the timeCodesPerSecond values conflict
It scales the time samples automatically so the referenced animation keeps its real-time duration
explanation: timeCodesPerSecond is automatically reconciled: USD scales the referenced time samples so the 60 fps animation preserves its real-time duration and motion in the 24 fps scene - unlike metersPerUnit, which is not auto-reconciled. The samples are not composed literally (so no 2.5x speedup occurs), composition is not skipped over conflicting timing metadata, and no clamping to the scene's time code range takes place.

stem: A two-quad mesh has 6 points and 2 faces. A displayColor primvar is authored with 'vertex' interpolation. How many color values must its array contain?
choices: 2 values (one per face)
6 values (one per point)
1 value (one for the whole gprim)
8 values (one per faceVertex index)
explanation: Vertex interpolation authors one value per point (vertex) of the mesh. This mesh has 6 points, so the array needs 6 values. Constant would be 1 (whole gprim), uniform would be 2 (per face), and faceVarying would be 8 (per faceVertex index).

stem: A developer authors a custom attribute with custom=True. What effect does the custom=True flag have on how OpenUSD treats that attribute?
choices: It registers the attribute with the schema registry so USD treats it as a builtin property
It has no effect on how USD treats the attribute; it signals the attribute is not part of a schema
It prevents opinions in stronger layers from overriding the attribute's authored value
It marks the attribute as animatable so that USD permits time samples to be authored on it
explanation: Setting custom=True has no impact on how OpenUSD treats the attribute; it is informational metadata telling end-users and developers that the attribute is not part of an existing schema. It does not register anything with the schema registry, it does not shield the value from stronger-layer overrides, and animatability is independent of the flag - attributes can hold time samples regardless.

stem: An integration must attach grouped sensor readings (temperature, humidity, pressure) to one prim, but USD has no native struct type. What is the standard convention for such structured data?
choices: Author namespace-prefixed attributes such as acme:sensor:temperature to group the related fields on the prim
Define a child prim per reading and author each value as a single attribute on its own prim
Author a relationship per reading that targets a separate prim holding the corresponding value
Serialize the readings into one string attribute that downstream tools parse back into fields
explanation: Since USD has no native struct type, namespace-prefixed attributes (acme:sensor:temperature, acme:sensor:humidity, acme:sensor:pressure) are the standard convention for grouped data: the nested prefixes keep related fields together on one prim and identify their origin. Splitting fields across child prims or pointing at value prims through relationships scatters the data instead of grouping it on the prim, and serializing into one string hides the values from typed access.

stem: Hydra decouples scene data from rendering backends. Which trio correctly names Hydra's three main parts and their roles?
choices: Scene delegate (provides scene information), render index (tracks changes and manages the scene), render delegate (produces the final image)
Scene delegate (tracks changes and manages the scene), render index (provides scene information), render delegate (produces the final image)
Scene delegate (produces the final image), render index (tracks changes and manages the scene), render delegate (provides scene information)
Scene delegate (provides scene information), render index (produces the final image), render delegate (tracks changes and manages the scene)
explanation: Hydra's scene delegate provides the scene information, its render index keeps track of changes and manages the scene, and its render delegate uses the render index and scene delegate to produce the final image for a specific backend. The other pairings swap these roles: the render index neither provides scene information nor produces the image, and the scene delegate neither manages the scene nor renders the final image.

stem: OpenUSD ships with a render delegate that provides an out-of-the-box, real-time way to visualize USD data (used by usdview and many tools). Which render delegate is this?
choices: RenderMan — the default render delegate included with OpenUSD
Arnold — the production path tracer bundled with OpenUSD
HdStorm — the OpenGL/Metal/Vulkan render delegate shipped with OpenUSD
HdEmbree — the example render delegate used as the default viewport renderer
explanation: HdStorm is the real-time OpenGL/Metal/Vulkan render delegate that ships with OpenUSD and is leveraged by usdview and many other tools. Arnold and RenderMan are third-party renderers Hydra supports but does not bundle, and HdEmbree ships (alongside HdTiny) as an example of how to implement a render delegate, not as the default viewport renderer.

stem: For the DistantLight below with only a rotation authored, along which local axis does a UsdLuxDistantLight emit by default, before any transform is applied?
choices: Along +Y (up)
Along +X
Radially in all directions
Along the -Z axis
explanation: A UsdLuxDistantLight emits from a distant source along the -Z axis, which is why it is commonly used as a directional light (e.g. a sun). Orienting the sun in a scene is done by rotating the light prim (e.g. via XformCommonAPI.SetRotate).

stem: A geometry prim's visibility attribute resolves to 'invisible'. How does this differ from deactivating the prim, and what is the effect on its subtree?
choices: Both remove the prim and its subtree from composition, so neither remains queryable on the stage
Invisible prunes just the prim itself from rendering; deactivation prunes the prim together with its descendants
Invisible prunes the prim and its subtree from rendering but leaves them composed; deactivation removes them from composition
Invisible removes the prim and its subtree from composition; deactivation merely skips them at render time
explanation: An invisible resolved value is pruning - neither the prim nor anything in its subtree is rendered - but the geometry remains composed on the stage and available for inspection and positioning, whereas deactivation removes the prim and its descendants from composition entirely. The two are not equivalent, invisibility is not limited to the prim alone, and it is deactivation rather than invisibility that removes prims from composition.

stem: In a USD scene a Scope prim is used to group all material prims. Which statement about Scope is correct?
choices: A Scope inherits from UsdGeomXformable, so it can carry animated transform ops like an Xform prim
A Scope is a non-transformable grouping prim; transformable children below it still evaluate correctly
A Scope requires a Gprim descendant before it composes as a valid organizational prim on the stage
A Scope applies its authored transform to child prims during stage evaluation
explanation: Scope is a grouping primitive that does not have transformability - like an empty folder - and transformable child prims such as Xforms and geometry are still evaluated correctly within and below it. Scope does not inherit from UsdGeomXformable, it has no transform of its own to apply to children, and it is valid as a purely organizational container with no Gprim requirement.

stem: For the Xform below authored via XformCommonAPI, what xformOpOrder does the API author, and in what order are the component transforms applied?

snippets.code:
def Xform "Parent_Prim"
{
    float3 xformOp:rotateXYZ = (90, 0, 0)
    float3 xformOp:scale = (3, 3, 3)
    double3 xformOp:translate = (5, 0, 3)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate", "xformOp:rotateXYZ", "xformOp:scale"]
}

choices: A fixed order — [xformOp:translate, xformOp:rotateXYZ, xformOp:scale] — translate, then rotate, then scale
An arbitrary order — xformOpOrder is authored as whatever permutation the caller requests
A single op — one xformOp:transform matrix combining translate, rotate, and scale
A fixed order — [xformOp:scale, xformOp:rotateXYZ, xformOp:translate] — scale, then rotate, then translate
explanation: XformCommonAPI restricts authoring to a fixed, standard op order - [xformOp:translate, xformOp:rotateXYZ, xformOp:scale], plus an optional pivot - which is what keeps transforms easily interchangeable across DCC tools. It does not accept arbitrary permutations, it authors component ops rather than a single matrix op, and a scale-first order is the reverse of what it writes.

stem: Which statements correctly describe how IsA (typed) schemas versus API schemas are assigned to and identified on a prim?
choices: API schemas are list-edited into the apiSchemas metadata and queried with HasAPI(); they assign no typeName
A multiple-apply API schema can be applied several times to the same prim with different instance names
An IsA schema may be abstract or concrete, and both kinds can be instantiated directly as prims
An IsA schema is assigned via the typeName metadata, and a prim can subscribe to only one IsA schema at a time
API schema properties share the prim's top-level namespace rather than carrying a schema-specific prefix
explanation: API schemas assign no typeName, are list-edited into apiSchemas, and are queried via HasAPI(); a multiple-apply API schema can be applied repeatedly with distinct instance names; and an IsA schema is assigned via typeName, with each prim subscribing to only one at a time. The claim that both abstract and concrete typed schemas can be instantiated is wrong because abstract schemas provide no typeName and serve only as base classes like UsdGeomPointBased. The namespace claim is wrong because API schema properties are namespaced with the schema's prefix (for example physics:velocity) rather than sharing the prim's top-level namespace.

stem: A concrete IsA schema and an abstract IsA schema differ in their schema definitions. What distinguishes a concrete typed schema from an abstract (non-concrete) one?
choices: An abstract schema can be instantiated as prims, while a concrete schema serves only as a base class for derived schemas
A concrete schema is generated as a codeless schema, while an abstract schema ships with compiled C++ and Python classes
A concrete schema is applied through the apiSchemas list, while an abstract schema is assigned through the typeName metadata
A concrete schema provides a name and a typeName and can be instantiated as prims, while an abstract schema has no typeName and serves as a base class
explanation: Concrete typed schemas provide both a name and a typeName and can be instantiated as prims (for example UsdGeomMesh), while abstract typed schemas provide a name but no typeName and serve as base classes for related concrete schemas (for example UsdGeomPointBased). The instantiation claim with abstract schemas instantiable and concrete ones serving as base classes is the exact inversion. Codeless versus compiled code generation is orthogonal to the concrete/abstract distinction. And neither kind of typed schema is applied through the apiSchemas list; that mechanism belongs to API schemas.

stem: A studio wants to traverse only the active, loaded prims of a large stage and combine those two predicates. Which approach is correct, and what is the key caution?
choices: Call Traverse() once per predicate and intersect the results manually, since each range accepts a single predicate
Use TraverseAll() with no predicate, since it already restricts traversal to active and loaded prims
Combine them with bitwise operators (Usd.PrimIsActive & Usd.PrimIsLoaded), since Python's and/or/not do not combine predicates
Combine them with Python boolean operators (Usd.PrimIsActive and Usd.PrimIsLoaded), since predicates evaluate as plain booleans
explanation: Traversal predicates must be combined with bitwise operators (&, |, ~), as in Usd.PrimIsActive & Usd.PrimIsLoaded; Python's and/or/not do not combine predicates correctly, which is the key caution. Predicates do not evaluate as plain booleans for this purpose, so the boolean-operator approach silently misbehaves. Running multiple traversals and intersecting results is unnecessary because a single traversal accepts a combined predicate. And TraverseAll() does the opposite of restricting: it visits all prims, including inactive and unloaded ones.

stem: During a Usd.PrimRange traversal, a tool reaches a prim named 'Environment' and wants to skip visiting all of its descendants without stopping the overall traversal. Which mechanism does this?
choices: Call TraverseAll() instead of Traverse() to change which prims the range visits
Switch the iterator to PreAndPostVisit mode to control descent into children
Set the Environment prim's active metadata to false to drop it from the range
Call PruneChildren() on the iterator to skip the current prim's children
explanation: Usd.PrimRange.PruneChildren(), invoked on the iterator, skips all children of the current prim while the rest of the traversal continues. TraverseAll() changes which prims are eligible across the whole stage rather than skipping one subtree mid-iteration. PreAndPostVisit mode visits each prim twice (entering and exiting) but does not skip descendants. Deactivating the prim would prune it, but it is a persistent scene-description edit, not an in-flight traversal control.

stem: A pipeline sets the 'active' metadata of /World/Box to false. The stage is then traversed with the default Traverse(). What happens to /World/Box and its descendants, and is the change destructive?
choices: The default traversal skips Box, but its descendants remain composed on the stage and visible to consumers
Box and its descendants are erased from the layer's scene description, so restoring them requires re-authoring the prims
Box itself is skipped but its descendants still compose, since deactivation applies one level deep
Box and all of its descendants are pruned from traversal and composition; the change is non-destructive and reversible
explanation: Deactivation prunes the prim and all of its descendants from both default traversals and composition, so Box, Geometry, Cube, Materials, and BoxMat all disappear from the composed view, yet the operation is non-destructive: the scene description still exists and the prim can be re-activated. It is not a traversal-only effect, because descendants are not composed onto the stage at all. It is not an erasure, because nothing is removed from the layer. And it is not shallow, because the prune applies to the entire subtree, not just one level.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Active and Inactive Prims

stem: A team is choosing among the native OpenUSD file formats. Which statements are correct?
choices: USDC (Crate) is a compressed binary format optimized for fast loading and heavy numeric data, while USDA is human-readable ASCII
USDZ is an atomic, uncompressed zipped archive intended as read-only packaging/delivery, ideal for XR
A .usd file may be either ASCII or binary, so the underlying encoding can change without breaking references
The four native formats are the complete set of file formats that USD stages can read; other 3D formats require conversion to USD first
USDA is the recommended production format for large data-heavy geometry layers because text opens faster than binary
explanation: USDC is the compressed binary Crate format suited to fast loading and numerically heavy data while USDA is human-readable ASCII; USDZ is an atomic, uncompressed zipped archive meant as read-only packaging and delivery, ideal for XR; and a .usd file can be either encoding, so it can change without breaking references. The completeness claim is wrong because any other 3D format can be loaded through file format plugins without prior conversion. The USDA-for-heavy-geometry claim is wrong because binary crate, not ASCII text, is preferred for large geometry layers.

stem: A statement claims: 'Even .usdc, .usd, .usda, and .usdz are themselves file format plugins, and any other 3D file format can be loaded into USD stages through plugins.' Is this accurate?
