choices: Yes — the native formats are themselves file format plugins, and any data provider can implement one so its format speaks USD natively
No — foreign formats are read through ArResolver implementations, while the four native formats are compiled into the core
Partially — USDZ is implemented as a package plugin, while .usd, .usda, and .usdc are compiled into the Sdf core library
No — file format plugins exist for adding new formats, but the four native formats are built into the USD core rather than implemented as plugins
explanation: The statement is accurate: even .usdc, .usd, .usda, and .usdz are implemented as file format plugins, and any data provider can implement a file format plugin so its format natively speaks USD. ArResolver handles asset path resolution, not reading foreign file contents, so that mechanism is misattributed. Neither the claim that only USDZ is a plugin nor the claim that all four native formats are built into the core matches the documentation, which singles out the native formats as plugins themselves.

stem: A developer is mapping out which core OpenUSD module to use for a task. Which module pairing is correct?
choices: UsdGeom is the core module for opening stages and composing prims; Usd holds the geometry schemas for meshes and curves
Sdf is the client-facing module for opening stages and editing prims; Usd provides layer serialization and path management
Usd is the client-facing module for authoring and reading stages and prims; Sdf provides scene-description foundations such as SdfLayer and paths
Gf provides prim and property path management; Sdf supplies the linear-algebra types for matrices and vectors
explanation: Usd is the core client-facing module for authoring, composing, and reading USD, including creating or opening a stage and working with prims, properties, metadata, and arcs, while Sdf provides the scene-description foundations such as SdfLayer and prim/property path management. The pairing that gives Sdf the stage-facing role and Usd the serialization role swaps the two modules. UsdGeom is the geometry schema domain, not the stage-opening module. And Gf supplies math/linear-algebra types, not path management, which is the reverse of the remaining pairing.

stem: Using Sdf.Path string syntax, which separators correctly introduce a child prim, a property, and a variant selection, respectively?
choices: A period (.) for a child prim, a colon (:) for a property, and a slash (/) for a variant
A backslash (\) for a child prim, a period (.) for a property, and parentheses for a variant
A forward slash (/) for a child prim, a period (.) for a property, and curly braces ({}) for a variant selection
A colon (:) for a child prim, a slash (/) for a property, and brackets ([]) for a variant
explanation: In Sdf.Path syntax: a forward slash (/) separates prim names in namespace (e.g. /geo/box); a period (.) after an identifier introduces a property (e.g. /geo/box.weight); and variants are indicated by curly braces (e.g. /geo/box{size=large}). The colon (:) is used within a property name for namespaced properties, not as a path separator between prims.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Prim and Property Paths

stem: A scene uses scenegraph instancing for many identical prims that share one prototype, and you need to add variety to a subset. Which refinement techniques cause OpenUSD to create a new prototype as a result of the edit?
choices: Ad hoc arcs refinement, by adding a new composition arc to the instanceable prim on the local layer stack
Refinement using variant sets, by making a different variant selection on the instanceable prim
Deinstancing refinement, by setting instanceable = false on a single instance
Broadcasted refinement, by authoring a new opinion on a shared inherit or specialize target
Hierarchical refinement, by authoring an inherited primvar opinion on an ancestor prim
explanation: Variant set refinement is evaluated during composition, so a new variant selection makes OpenUSD figure out the additional implicit prototypes it needs (the exercise goes from 3 to 4 prototypes). Ad hoc arcs refinement adds a new composition arc on the instanceable prim; because prototypes are built off composition arcs, introducing a new arc triggers a new prototype shared by instances using that arc. Broadcasted refinement authors opinions on an inherit/specialize target, producing a new prototype shared among instances that received the change. Hierarchical refinement using inherited primvars/xformOps/visibility explicitly does NOT create new prototypes—it only adds opinions on the already-counted instanceable prims. Deinstancing does not create a new prototype either; it disables instancing for that copy, increasing the total prim count linearly while leaving the prototype count unchanged.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Ad Hoc Arcs Refinement

stem: A team is reviewing the rules of instance editability before refining a scene that uses scenegraph instancing. Which statements about editing scenegraph instances are correct?
choices: Authoring an over on a /__Prototype_01 prim seen in the tree view is the correct way to edit the prototype
Prototypes are an editable runtime data model that can be overridden directly on the local layer stack
Every prim under an instanceable prim can be freely overridden because the instance root is editable
The xformOp:translate opinion on the instanceable prim /World/RobotArm_01 is a valid, editable override
The over on /World/RobotArm_01/joint_1 is invalid because it targets an instance proxy, whose local opinions are discarded
explanation: The three rules are: prototypes are a runtime data model and are not editable; instance proxies are not editable and their local opinions are discarded; instanceable prims are editable. Thus the xformOp:translate on the instanceable prim /World/RobotArm_01 is a valid override, while the over on joint_1 (an instance proxy) is invalid. Authoring an over on a /__Prototype_01 item produces a dangling override unrelated to the actual prototype, so that choice is wrong. Prototypes are not editable, contradicting the fourth choice. The instance root being editable does not make its descendant instance proxies editable, so the last choice is wrong.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Scenegraph Instance Refinement

stem: A technical artist must refine a UsdGeomPointInstancer that scatters thousands of instances after a physics simulation. Which statements about refining point instances are correct?
choices: Introducing an additional prototype is automatic and requires no changes to the prototypes relationship or protoIndices
Use inactiveIds metadata to prune an instance entirely, and it can be list-edited to sparsely add and remove ids
Promotion turns a point instance into a fully editable subgraph without first deactivating the original point
Setting instanceable = false on a chosen point is the standard way to prune a single point instance
Use the invisibleIds attribute when you need to animate an instance on and off over time
explanation: The guidance states you prune or hide instances using inactiveIds metadata and the invisibleIds attribute respectively, and the rule of thumb is to use invisibleIds when you need to animate an instance on and off over time, otherwise use inactiveIds; inactiveIds can also be list-edited to sparsely add and remove ids. Introducing a new prototype is NOT automatic—point instancing's explicit prototype pattern requires defining a new prim hierarchy, adding it to the prototypes relationship, and updating protoIndices. Promotion starts with pruning (deactivating the point) and then replacing it with the full asset, so it does begin by deactivating the point. instanceable is a scenegraph-instancing concept, not how point instances are pruned.

stem: When choosing between scenegraph instancing and point instancing, which statements correctly characterize point instancing?
choices: It is schema-based instancing with explicit prototypes specified in the scene description
It is the preferred choice for reusing complex components such as shelf assemblies and robots
It offers transparent deinstancing that requires no scene description changes, like scenegraph instancing
It is well suited to massive numbers of simpler items where per-instance overhead outweighs reuse benefits
Its instances are identifiable via scene description path, like scenegraph instances
explanation: Point instancing is schema-based with explicit prototypes specified in scene description, and it is good for massive numbers of simpler items, such as leaves on trees, where the overhead of a full instance outweighs the benefits of reuse. Reusing complex components like shelf assemblies and robots is a scenegraph instancing strength. Point-instance deinstancing is invasive, not transparent, and its instances are identified by index, not by scene description path; both of those properties belong to scenegraph instancing.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: OpenUSD Instancing Frequently Asked Questions

stem: A developer is implementing a UsdGeomPointInstancer in a converter and must author every property that the schema treats as required. Which properties are the required properties of UsdGeomPointInstancer?
choices: invisibleIds
positions
orientations
protoIndices
prototypes
explanation: In the UsdGeomPointInstancer schema, GetProtoIndicesAttr, GetPositionsAttr, and GetPrototypesRel are each documented as a 'Required property.' The orientations, scales, velocities, accelerations, angularVelocities, ids, and invisibleIds members are all optional—their documentation says they only take effect 'if authored.' Therefore orientations and invisibleIds are distractors that are optional, not required.

stem: A team is designing a two-phase (extract, then transform) OpenUSD data-exchange converter. Which statements about the two phases are correct?
choices: Extraction output should be written to disk as a persistent intermediate rather than treated as transient data
Export options should be implemented as part of the extraction phase rather than as data transformation
Round-trip workflows benefit from applying as many transformations as possible during export
The transform phase consists of one or more optional steps, such as applying export options and restructuring content for end clients
The extract phase should translate the source data to OpenUSD as directly as possible to maintain fidelity to the source format
explanation: The extract phase should translate source data to OpenUSD as directly as possible to maintain fidelity, and the transform phase is one or more optional steps such as applying user export options and changing content structure to better meet end-client needs. Extraction output is often transient and need not persist to disk, so the persistent-intermediate guidance is wrong. Export options are best thought of as data transformation, not extraction. And round-trip workflows call for minimizing transformations, since extensive ones complicate reversing changes accurately.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Exchange?

stem: A studio is organizing assets into parallel workstreams using OpenUSD layer stacks. Which practices are recommended?
choices: Computational workstreams should remain static and consistent from one evaluation of the stage to the next
Simple assets should be split into separate workstream layers up front so parallelism is available later
Layer stacks should be kept simple, avoiding workstreams that grow procedurally, since each layer has a resolve-and-open cost
Each workstream should author only its unique contributions sparsely rather than overwriting other workstreams' work
Layer stacks should serve as the asset versioning mechanism, with each version captured as a sublayer
explanation: The guidance is to keep layer stacks simple and manageable, avoiding workstreams that might grow procedurally over time because each layer carries a resolve-and-open cost, and to have each workstream author only its unique contributions sparsely rather than needlessly overwriting another workstream's work. Layer stacks are explicitly not a replacement for asset versioning systems, so capturing versions as sublayers is wrong. Simple assets can live in a single layer, so pre-splitting them is wrong. And computational workstreams can be dynamic, not necessarily consistent between evaluations.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Modeling Workstreams With Layer Stacks

stem: Which statements correctly describe how sublayers behave within a layer stack?
choices: When a layer is composed as a sublayer, its contents are added to the destination layer in an "include" fashion without path remapping.
Sublayers are an ordered list where the first listed layer is stronger than the last listed layer.
Sublayer opinions are weaker than opinions delivered through references composed in the same layer stack.
For the same property, an opinion in a later-listed sublayer overrides one in an earlier-listed sublayer.
Each sublayer is grafted onto a single destination prim, undergoing a prim name change and path translation.
explanation: Sublayers are an ordered list with the first layer strongest and the last weakest, and a composed sublayer contributes its contents in an "include" fashion without path remapping. Sublayer opinions are local and therefore stronger, not weaker, than opinions delivered through references. A later-listed sublayer does not override an earlier one, since earlier entries are stronger. And grafting onto a destination prim with a name change and path translation describes references, not sublayers.

stem: What is true about references as a composition arc?
choices: References graft a prim hierarchy from one layer onto a prim of another layer, making them ideal for modularity and reusability.
A referenced prim keeps its original name and path unchanged when grafted into the new namespace.
A reference can be external, targeting a prim from a different layer, or internal, targeting a prim within the same layer.
Sublayering a layer multiple times is the recommended way to create multiple sibling copies of the same content.
Referenced content can be unloaded on demand at runtime to defer its loading.
explanation: References graft a prim hierarchy from one layer onto a prim of another layer for modularity and reuse, and they can be external (targeting a prim in a different layer) or internal (targeting a prim within the same layer). The ability to load and unload on demand is the distinguishing feature of payloads, not references, which are always composed and present on the stage. Sublayering a layer multiple times will not create siblings because there is no way to specify different paths, so references are used instead. The referenced prim undergoes a prim name change and path translation to reflect the new namespace, so it does not keep its original name and path.

stem: How do payloads differ from references in OpenUSD?
choices: Payload composition arcs can be applied to the same prim in a list-editable way, just like references.
Unloading a payload recomposes the prim but leaves all descendant prims of the payloaded prim loaded.
Payloads are weaker than references in the LIVERPS composition strength order.
Payloads can be loaded and unloaded on demand, while references are always composed and present on the stage.
Payloads are stronger than references, so a payload opinion overrides a competing referenced opinion.
explanation: Payloads can be loaded and unloaded on demand whereas references are always composed and present on the stage, payloads are weaker than references in the LIVERPS strength order, and payload arcs can be applied to the same prim in a list-editable way just like references. The reversed strength claim is wrong because payloads sit below references, so a payload opinion does not override a competing referenced opinion. And unloading a payload recomposes the prim and removes the descendants of the payloaded prim from the stage, so they are not left loaded.

stem: A variant within a variant set can do which of the following inside its prim hierarchy?
choices: Define new descendant prims that exist only when that variant is selected.
Author new composition arcs, such as a reference, that exist only within that variant.
Sparsely override properties on the owning prim's ancestor or sibling prims.
Sparsely override properties on the prim or any descendant prim.
Compose the opinions of every variant in the set simultaneously onto the stage.
explanation: A variant can sparsely override properties on the prim or any of its descendants, define new descendant prims, and author new composition arcs such as a reference that exist only within that variant. A variant set is added to a prim and its variants manipulate that prim and its descendants, so they cannot reach ancestor or sibling prims outside that hierarchy. And only the selected variant's opinions compose onto the stage, never every variant at once.

stem: When designing variant sets for real-time switching, which variant operations are considered heavyweight because they require rebuilding parts of the composition index?
choices: Changing a prim's visibility to hide or show geometry.
Changing an attribute value, such as switching a color from red to blue.
Changing a numeric parameter on an existing prim.
Changing which reference paths (layer files) are brought into the scene.
Changing activation opinions that activate or deactivate prims.
explanation: Heavyweight variant switches change the composition structure itself: changing reference paths swaps which layer files are brought into the scene, and changing activation opinions affects what gets composed, both forcing USD to recompute parts of its composition index. Changing an attribute value, changing visibility, and changing a numeric parameter are lightweight because they only affect value resolution; the composition index stays the same and only the final resolved values change.

stem: Which statements about inherit arcs and the class specifier they are typically authored with are correct?
choices: Hydra does not image (render) a prim with a class specifier or any of its descendants.
An inherit arc creates an isolated copy of the source so later edits to the source do not propagate to inheriting prims.
An opinion authored on the source prim in one scenario automatically affects every other scenario that uses the asset.
A prim with a class specifier is imaged by Hydra, while its descendants are skipped during traversal.
Modifications to the inherit source prim are broadcast and applied to all prims that inherit it within the context where the change is authored.
explanation: Inherit arcs broadcast modifications of the source prim to all inheriting prims within the context where the change is authored, and Hydra does not image a prim with a class specifier or any of its descendants. The claim that the class prim itself is imaged while only its descendants are skipped inverts that rule, since neither is rendered. Inherits do not create isolated copies, which is what references do, and an opinion authored in one scenario affects only that context, not every other scenario that uses the asset.

stem: Which statements correctly describe local (L) opinions and the layer stack in LIVERPS strength ordering?
choices: Sublayers of sublayers belong to a separate layer stack and are evaluated only after references are resolved.
In LIVERPS ordering, local opinions are the strongest and specialize arcs are the weakest.
References and payloads contribute local opinions, because their layers join the root layer stack once composed.
Opinions authored directly in a root layer and in any of its recursive sublayers are all considered local opinions of that layer stack.
A layer stack is the ordered set of layers from recursively gathering all sublayers, plus the layer itself as first and strongest.
explanation: A layer stack is the ordered set of layers gathered recursively from all sublayers plus the layer itself as first and strongest, opinions authored in the root layer or any recursive sublayer are all local to that stack, and in LIVERPS local opinions are strongest while specialize arcs are weakest. Layers brought in by references and payloads form their own separate layer stacks, so their opinions are not local to the root stack. And sublayers of sublayers belong to the same layer stack, contributing local opinions rather than being evaluated after references.

stem: When debugging why a composed prim or property has an unexpected value, which statements about the prim stack and property stack are correct?
choices: The property stack always contains the correct time-offsets for animated values even when layer offsets are present.
GetPrimStack() returns only the single strongest prim spec, discarding all weaker contributing specs.
The prim stack and property stack are the recommended high-performance path for repeatedly resolving an attribute value.
UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack() should only be used for debugging, not for value resolution.
UsdPrim::GetPrimStack() returns the ordered list of prim specs across layers that contribute opinions to a prim's metadata.
explanation: GetPrimStack() returns the ordered list of prim specs across layers that contribute opinions to a prim's metadata, and GetPropertyStack() should only be used for debugging, not for value resolution. The property stack does not contain the correct time-offsets for animated values when layer offsets are present, so that claim is wrong. For optimized repeated value resolution you should retain a UsdAttributeQuery rather than use the stacks. And GetPrimStack() returns all contributing prim specs in strength order, not just the single strongest one.

stem: When troubleshooting performance and unexpected resolved values, which statements about composition versus value resolution are correct?
choices: Composition is cached as a prim-level index when a stage is opened or edited, but value resolution is not pre-calculated.
Value resolution pre-calculates and stores every property's final value at stage open for fast repeated access.
If you need to get the same attribute value many times efficiently, you can cache it yourself using UsdAttributeQuery.
Querying an attribute with Get() and no time code is always equivalent to using Usd.TimeCode.EarliestTime().
Composition rules vary by data type, while value resolution rules vary by composition arc.
explanation: When a stage is opened or data is added, USD creates an index of the composition logic and result at the prim level, but it does not pre-calculate final property values, which keeps the system fast and memory-light. To repeatedly resolve the same attribute value efficiently you can cache it yourself with UsdAttributeQuery. The rule about what varies is reversed: composition rules vary by composition arc while value resolution rules vary by data type. Value resolution is not pre-calculated at stage open, and Get() with no time code is equivalent to Usd.TimeCode.Default(), not EarliestTime().

stem: While isolating a problematic part of a large stage, which statements about deactivating prims are correct?
choices: Deactivating a prim removes its specs from the underlying scene description, so restoring it requires re-authoring the prim.
An inactive prim itself is still visited by default stage traversals, while its descendant prims are skipped and not composed.
A deactivated prim's inactive state can be overridden by a stronger layer opinion that sets "active" to true, allowing selective reactivation.
Setting a prim's "active" metadata to false is a non-destructive prune that excludes the prim and its descendants from being composed onto the stage.
Deactivation marks the prim as hidden for render delegates while it and its descendants continue to compose onto the stage.
explanation: Setting "active" to false is a non-destructive prune that excludes the prim and its descendants from composition, and because the scene description persists, a stronger layer opinion can set "active" back to true to selectively reactivate the pruned subtree. Deactivation removes no specs from the layer, so nothing has to be re-authored to restore the prim. An inactive prim is itself excluded from default traversals, not visited with its descendants skipped. And deactivation operates at the composition level rather than as a render-delegate visibility flag, so the prim and its descendants are not composed at all.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Active and Inactive Prims

stem: File format plugins are a unique OpenUSD feature for adding support for other data formats. Which statements about file format plugins are correct?
choices: They support reading from the source format but not writing translated USD data back to it.
They keep the translated USD copy, rather than the source file, as the ongoing source of truth.
They allow OpenUSD to compose with non-file-based sources such as databases and procedurally generated content.
They require the source file to be rewritten to USDC before it can be referenced onto a stage.
A source file format can be included in a stage as a reference, payload, or sublayer, translated on the fly as it is read.
explanation: Correct: file format plugins let a source format be included in a stage as a reference, payload, or sublayer, translated on the fly while read as a USD layer, and they let OpenUSD compose with non-file-based sources like databases and procedural content. Wrong: plugins can be bidirectional rather than read-only, the source file format can remain the source of truth instead of a translated copy, and no rewrite to USDC is required since translation happens on the fly.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Exchange?

stem: The two-phase data exchange approach is loosely inspired by Extract-Transform-Load (ETL). Which statements correctly describe the goals of the extract phase versus the transform phase?
choices: The transform phase should map source concepts to OpenUSD concepts as directly as possible to preserve source integrity.
The extract phase aims to translate data to OpenUSD as directly as possible to maintain fidelity to the source format.
The transform phase consists of optional steps, such as export options and content restructuring, to better meet end-client needs.
The extract phase is where user export options should be applied to conform the output to a destination format.
The extract phase is where optimizations such as mesh merging are applied for end-client performance.
explanation: Correct: extraction translates data to OpenUSD as directly as possible to maintain fidelity to the source, and the transform phase is one or more optional steps such as export options and content restructuring that better meet end-client needs. Wrong: direct mapping for source integrity is the goal of extraction rather than transformation, and both export options and optimizations like mesh merging belong to the transform phase, not extraction.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Data Exchange?

stem: A team is choosing native USD file formats for an exchange pipeline. Which statements about USDA, USDC, and USDZ are correct?
choices: USDA files are ASCII text that are human-readable, making them optimal for small files such as a stage referencing external content.
USDC (the Crate Binary Format) is designed to minimize load time and is extremely efficient for numerically-heavy data like geometry.
USDZ is an atomic, zipped archive that packages assets together, is generally intended as read-only, and is optimal for XR experiences.
USDZ files are editable working archives, making them the preferred format while an asset is still being actively modified.
USDA is the Crate binary format, designed for memory mapping and fast parsing of numerically-heavy geometry data.
explanation: Correct: USDA is human-readable ASCII suited to small files like a stage referencing external content; USDC is the Crate Binary Format built to minimize load time for numerically-heavy data; USDZ is an atomic zipped archive, generally read-only, that packages assets and suits XR delivery. Wrong: USDZ is not an editable working format and would not be used while still making edits, and USDA is plain text, not the Crate binary format (that is USDC).

stem: Running usdchecker on a freshly converted obj2usd asset reports three errors related to stage metadata, then a transformation step is added. Which statements about usdchecker and the Omniverse Asset Validator are correct?
choices: usdchecker is part of the USD Toolset and validates a stage or USDZ package against defined rules for interchange and Hydra renderability.
usdchecker validates standalone USDA text layers but has no support for inspecting packaged USDZ archives.
The Omniverse Asset Validator implements its own rule engine that is developed separately from usdchecker's rule set.
usdchecker automatically rewrites the converter's extraction code to author whatever stage metadata is missing.
The Omniverse Asset Validator is based on usdchecker, adding automatic fixes for failed validations and the ability to add new rules.
explanation: Correct: usdchecker is part of the USD Toolset and validates a USD stage or USDZ package against defined rules to assure interchangeability and Hydra renderability, and the Omniverse Asset Validator is based on usdchecker while adding automatic fixes and the ability to add new rules. Wrong: usdchecker does inspect USDZ packages, the Asset Validator builds on usdchecker's rules rather than maintaining a separate engine, and usdchecker reports problems but never rewrites converter code.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Asset Validation?

stem: During the obj2usd transform phase, a chaser reparents all root prims under a new /World prim. Given the snippet, which statements correctly explain why this transformation is needed?

snippets.code:
def set_default_prim(stage: Usd.Stage):
    root_prims = stage.GetPseudoRoot().GetChildren()
    world_prim = UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/World").GetPrim()
    stage.SetDefaultPrim(world_prim)
    editor = Usd.NamespaceEditor(stage)
    for prim in root_prims:
        editor.ReparentPrim(prim, world_prim)
        editor.ApplyEdits()

choices: The prims that make up the asset shared no common ancestor, so there was no easy way to reference the entire asset.
The converter output had no defaultPrim metadata, so the stage could not be referenced without specifying a target prim.
OBJ already defines a scene-graph root, so the /World prim simply renames the root that extraction produced.
Reparenting the prims under /World lets the geometry compress more efficiently into the USDC crate format.
Setting a defaultPrim satisfies the upAxis and metersPerUnit checks that usdchecker reported earlier.
explanation: Correct: the flat extracted output had no defaultPrim, so the stage could not be referenced without naming a target prim, and even with one set the asset's prims shared no common ancestor, so the whole asset could not be referenced together; /World plus reparenting fixes both. Wrong: OBJ has no scene-graph root so /World is a genuinely new ancestor rather than a rename, reparenting has no effect on crate compression, and defaultPrim is unrelated to the upAxis and metersPerUnit metadata fixed during extraction.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Transforming the Prim Hierarchy

stem: A developer authors the displayColor primvar with interpolation set to "uniform" on a two-quad mesh. Which statements about primvar interpolation modes in OpenUSD are correct?
choices: "uniform" interpolation assigns one value per face of the primitive.
"uniform" interpolation assigns one value per point of the mesh.
"constant" interpolation assigns a single value for the whole gprim.
"constant" interpolation assigns one value per face of the primitive.
"vertex" interpolation assigns one value per point of the mesh.
explanation: Per the primvars lesson, the example builds the same two-quad mesh with three interpolation modes: constant (one value for the whole gprim), uniform (one value per face), and vertex (one value per point). So "uniform" assigning one value per face and "constant" assigning a single value for the whole gprim are both correct. The distractors invert these by claiming "uniform" is one value per point (that is actually vertex interpolation) and that "constant" is one value per face.

stem: Two sublayers author the same prim, with the stronger layer listed first. Which outcomes correctly describe how OpenUSD value resolution combines the different data types on that prim?
choices: For most metadata, the strongest opinion wins during composition.
Relationship targets combine opinions from all layers following list-editing rules.
Dictionary metadata like customData combines element by element, so keys authored only in the weaker layer still appear.
Relationship targets resolve to the strongest layer's target list, discarding the weaker layer's targets.
Metadata of every type combines element by element, regardless of the value's data type.
explanation: For most metadata the strongest opinion wins; relationship targets are combined from all layers following list-editing rules rather than a single winner being picked; and dictionary-valued metadata like customData merges per key, so keys authored only in the weaker layer persist. The statement that relationship targets discard the weaker layer's list contradicts list-edit combining, and element-by-element merging applies to dictionary types, not to metadata of every type.

stem: When querying a resolved attribute value in OpenUSD, which statements about attribute value resolution and time codes are correct?
choices: Using Usd.TimeCode.EarliestTime() returns the first authored time sample value when animation exists.
Calling Get() with no time code is equivalent to Get(Usd.TimeCode.Default()) and returns the authored default value.
Calling Get() with no time code returns the first authored time sample rather than the authored default value.
If no value is authored for an attribute, value resolution returns the nearest authored value from an ancestor prim.
Value resolution results are cached at the prim level in the same way composition results are cached.
explanation: Usd.TimeCode.EarliestTime() returns the first authored time sample when animation exists, and Get() with no time code is equivalent to Get(Usd.TimeCode.Default()), returning the authored default. The claim that a bare Get() returns the first time sample inverts that behavior; unauthored attributes resolve to the schema fallback, not to values from ancestor prims; and value resolution is not cached the way composition is.

stem: An OpenUSD developer is distinguishing IsA (typed) schemas from API schemas. Which statements are correct?
choices: API schemas do not assign a typeName; instead they are list-edited in the apiSchemas metadata and are queryable via the HasAPI method.
API schemas are assigned through the typeName metadata and are queryable via the IsA method, just like typed schemas.
A concrete IsA schema provides both a name and a typeName, while an abstract IsA schema provides a name but no typeName.
A prim may subscribe to several IsA schemas at once by list-editing them in the typeName metadata.
An IsA schema is assigned to a prim using the typeName metadata, and a prim can only subscribe to one IsA schema at a time.
explanation: API schemas do not assign a typeName - they are list-edited into the apiSchemas metadata and checked with HasAPI; concrete IsA schemas provide both a name and a typeName while abstract IsA schemas provide a name but no typeName; and an IsA schema is assigned via typeName, with a prim subscribing to one IsA schema at a time. The claims that API schemas use typeName and IsA, and that several IsA schemas can be list-edited into typeName, get this backwards: typeName holds a single type, and list-editing applies to apiSchemas.

stem: A developer is setting up rendering with Hydra in OpenUSD. Which statements about Hydra's architecture are correct?
choices: Hydra supports a single renderer per build, chosen when OpenUSD is compiled rather than swapped at runtime.
Hydra requires the scene data and the rendering backend to be compiled together as one tightly coupled module.
HdStorm is the real-time render delegate that ships with OpenUSD and is leveraged by usdview out of the box.
Hydra comprises a scene delegate (scene information), a render index (change tracking), and a render delegate (final image).
The render index is the component that provides the raw scene description to Hydra by loading it from disk.
explanation: HdStorm ships with OpenUSD as the real-time render delegate used by usdview, and Hydra's three parts are the scene delegate (provides scene information), the render index (tracks changes and manages the scene), and the render delegate (produces the final image). Hydra supports many render delegates selected at runtime rather than one renderer fixed at build time, it decouples scene data from the backend rather than coupling them, and scene information comes from the scene delegate, not from the render index loading it from disk.

stem: A lighting artist is working with the UsdLux schema domain. Which statements about UsdLux lights are correct?
choices: UsdLux has API schemas that let you add light behavior to existing prims such as meshes and volumes.
UsdLux lights are not Xformable, so they are aimed using shaping parameters rather than transform ops.
UsdLux provides standardized light types such as DistantLight, RectLight, DiskLight, SphereLight, and DomeLight.
UsdLux light types are concrete subclasses of UsdGeomMesh that render as emissive geometry by default.
UsdLuxDistantLight represents a directional light, emitting from a distant source along the -Z axis.
explanation: UsdLux includes API schemas that add light behavior to existing prims such as meshes and volumes, provides standardized light types including DistantLight, RectLight, DiskLight, SphereLight, and DomeLight, and its DistantLight emits from a distant source along the -Z axis as a directional light. Lights are Xformable - the lesson rotates and translates them via XformCommonAPI rather than aiming them through shaping parameters - and UsdLux light types belong to the UsdLux schema domain rather than subclassing UsdGeomMesh.

stem: A pipeline developer composes assets authored in different units into one scene so they display at correct scale. Which statements about how OpenUSD reconciles unit metadata during composition are correct?
choices: kilogramsPerUnit is automatically reconciled during composition in the same way that timeCodesPerSecond is reconciled.
metersPerUnit is automatically converted during composition, so a cube authored in centimeters appears at the correct size in a meter-based scene.
upAxis differences are automatically corrected by USD when layers authored with different up axes are composed.
timeCodesPerSecond is automatically reconciled during composition, so a referenced 60 fps animation plays back correctly in a 24 fps scene.
metersPerUnit is not automatically reconciled, so the assembler must apply corrective transforms when referenced geometry uses a different linear scale.
explanation: timeCodesPerSecond is auto-reconciled - USD scales time samples so a referenced 60 fps animation plays back correctly in a 24 fps scene - while metersPerUnit is not, so the assembler must add corrective transforms for differing linear scales. Geometric values are copied literally, so no automatic metersPerUnit conversion occurs; upAxis differences require manual coordinate transforms; and kilogramsPerUnit sits in the manually handled group, not the auto-reconciled one.

stem: A team is creating a custom schema for a proprietary data model rather than using ad-hoc custom properties. Which statements about custom schemas and OpenUSD's per-schema versioning are correct?
choices: Custom schemas group related information in a standardized way, but require more planning and take longer to implement than custom properties.
Custom schemas are easier and faster to set up than custom properties because they require no planning of predefined fields.
A schema's version must be stored as a separate metadata field on each prim rather than embedded in the type name.
All currently existing schemas are automatically considered version 0, which is represented without a version suffix.
A schema's version is embedded in the schema identifier itself as a suffix, for example "SphereLight_2" is version 2 of the SphereLight schema.
explanation: The custom properties lesson states custom schemas group related information and provide standardization but require more planning and take longer to implement than custom properties, and the Schema Versioning proposal states all currently existing schemas are automatically their own version 0 with no version suffix and that the version is embedded in the schema identifier as a suffix (e.g. "SphereLight_2" is version 2). The claim that custom schemas are easier and require no planning inverts the source, and the claim that the version must be a separate per-prim metadata field is wrong because the proposal explicitly decided against that, embedding the version in the type name instead.

stem: A developer adds proprietary data to prims using custom properties instead of a custom schema. Which statements about custom properties in OpenUSD are correct?

snippets.code:
#usda 1.0

def Xform "EnvironmentSensor"
{
    custom float acme:sensor:humidity = 45
    custom float acme:sensor:pressure = 101.3
    custom float acme:sensor:temperature = 22.5
}

choices: Namespace prefixes such as acme:sensor: are the standard convention for grouping related properties because USD has no native struct type.
Custom properties are predefined and standardized, unlike schema attributes which users can add at any time.
The custom=True flag forces OpenUSD to validate the attribute against a registered schema before authoring.
Custom attributes cannot hold arrays or be sampled over time, limiting them to single scalar values.
Setting custom=True has no impact on how OpenUSD treats the attribute; it is metadata signaling that the attribute is not part of an existing schema.
explanation: The custom properties lesson states that since USD has no native struct type, namespace-prefixed attributes such as acme:sensor: serve as the standard convention for grouping related data, and that setting custom=True has no impact on how OpenUSD treats the attribute but is useful metadata signaling it is not part of an existing schema. The claim that custom properties are predefined and standardized is false because they are user-defined (that description fits schema attributes), the claim that custom=True triggers schema validation is false, and the claim that custom attributes cannot hold arrays or be time-sampled is false because they can do both.

stem: A root layer authors no radius opinion. Its first (stronger) sublayer workstreamB.usd has no radius opinion; the weaker workstreamA.usd authors radius = 4.0. What radius resolves, and why?
choices: radius = 4.0; the weaker sublayer holds the only local opinion, so it wins because no stronger layer authors radius
radius = 4.0, because the last-listed sublayer is the strongest layer within a layer stack
No value; because workstreamB.usd is stronger and lacks an opinion, the property resolves to no authored value
No value; the root layer's over on Sphere blocks the weaker sublayer opinions from composing
explanation: All sublayers of the root belong to one layer stack, so their opinions are all local; USD walks the strength-ordered layers and a stronger layer that authors nothing simply contributes nothing, so workstreamA.usd holds the only radius opinion and 4.0 wins. The reason is not that the last-listed sublayer is strongest, since the first-listed is stronger but silent here. An empty stronger layer does not block the weaker opinion and yield no value. And an over spec never blocks opinions; it overlays without defining and lets composition proceed.

stem: On one prim a reference and an inherit arc each deliver a competing opinion for color, and a variant set is also selected that authors color. No local opinion exists. Under LIVERPS, which arc's color wins?
choices: The inherit arc, because inherits are evaluated before variant sets and references in LIVERPS ordering
The variant set, because the selected variant is evaluated immediately after local opinions
The reference arc, because references graft a full prim hierarchy and override broadcast arcs
The specialize arc, because the class source supplies the base value that the other arcs refine
explanation: LIVERPS orders arcs strongest to weakest as Local, Inherits, Variants, rElocates, References, Payloads, Specializes. With no local opinion, inherits is consulted before variant sets and references, so the inherited color wins. The selected variant is not evaluated immediately after local opinions, because inherits comes between them. References sit below both inherits and variants, so grafting a hierarchy gives them no override power here. And specializes is the weakest arc, supplying only a fallback when nothing else authors the value, not a winning base value.

stem: A class _cube_asset holds inputs:diffuseColor = (1,1,0) and a prim inherits it. A scene references the asset and overrides _cube_asset's color. What happens, and are other scenes referencing the asset affected?
choices: The override is dropped with a warning, because the class prim lies outside the referenced prim's hierarchy
The override is broadcast to every prim that inherits _cube_asset, but only within this scene's context; other scenes are unaffected
The override changes the single prim that authored the inherits arc; prims inheriting the class elsewhere keep the original color
The override is written into the asset's source layer, so every scene that references the asset picks up the new color
explanation: The inherit source acts like a globally editable class: overriding _cube_asset in the referencing scene broadcasts the new color to all prims that inherit it, but the broadcast applies only to the context where it is authored, so other scenes are unaffected. The override is not dropped even though the class sits outside the referenced hierarchy, because overriding a class across a reference is the intended workflow. It does not stop at the single prim holding the inherits arc, since inherits broadcasts. And it never edits the asset's source layer, which is why other referencing scenes keep the original color.

stem: Cubes inherit two classes: unencapsulated /_cube_asset and encapsulated /World/cube_pyramid_01/_local_cube. After the asset is referenced, overriding which class is a global refinement, and why?
choices: Neither class; inherit arc targets are re-pathed on reference, so both overrides stay local to their own subtree
/World/cube_pyramid_01/_local_cube; its encapsulated target path is re-pathed per reference, which broadcasts the override globally
Both classes; inherit targets are stored as absolute paths, so each override reaches every inheriting prim
/_cube_asset; its target path lies outside encapsulation and is never re-pathed on reference, so the override reaches every inheriting prim
explanation: Global refinement relies on an inherit target whose path never changes: /_cube_asset sits outside the encapsulated hierarchy, is never re-pathed on reference, and so overriding it reaches every inheriting prim. The encapsulated /World/cube_pyramid_01/_local_cube is re-pathed per reference, which makes its override a local refinement confined to one subtree, not a global broadcast. Not every inherit target is re-pathed, so the overrides do not all stay local. And the two classes do not behave identically merely because targets are written as absolute paths, since encapsulation determines whether re-pathing occurs.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Experimenting With Encapsulation and Refinement

stem: A class _cube_asset specializes diffuseColor = (1,0,0) onto three cubes. Two cubes author their own diffuseColor (blue, green). The class fallback is later changed to magenta. Which cubes turn magenta?
choices: Only the two cubes that authored their own color, because the new fallback overrides previously refined prims
None of the cubes, because each destination prim latches the fallback value present when the arc was authored
All three cubes, because the specializes source broadcasts to every destination prim
Only the cube with no authored diffuseColor; the two cubes with their own opinion ignore the changed fallback
explanation: Specializes applies the source's spec only where no other authored opinion exists, so the cube without its own diffuseColor adopts the magenta fallback while the refined blue and green cubes ignore the change. The fallback never overrides refined prims, so the two color-authoring cubes are not the ones that change. Destination prims do not latch the original fallback, because an updated class value does propagate to unrefined prims. And the broadcast does not recolor all three, since authored opinions are stronger than the specializes arc.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Experimenting With Specializes

stem: One variant on /Asset must pull in a blue material from a separate layer, not merely recolor an existing one. Which variant capability enables this, and what composes when that variant is inactive?
choices: A variant can define new prims inside the set, while composition arcs must be authored by a sublayer of the asset instead
A variant can author a new composition arc (a reference) that exists only in that variant; when inactive, that reference is not composed
A variant references the material globally, so the arc composes regardless of which variant is selected
A variant can override properties of an existing material, so the reference to the blue layer must already exist outside the variant
explanation: Variants can author new composition arcs that exist only within that variant, so one variant can reference the blue material from its separate layer, and when that variant is inactive the reference is simply not composed. Variants are not limited to defining prims while leaving arcs to sublayers, nor to overriding existing material properties with the reference forced to live outside the variant; both understate documented variant capabilities. And an arc authored inside a variant never composes regardless of selection, since it participates only while its variant is selected.

stem: Two variant sets exist on an asset: 'color' flips an attribute value, and 'lod' swaps which mesh file is referenced. For frequent real-time toggling, which set is preferable and why?
choices: 'lod', because changing reference paths is lighter than recomputing an attribute value
'lod', because swapping referenced files only re-resolves values without rebuilding composition
'color', because changing an attribute value only affects value resolution and leaves the composition index intact
Either; all variant switches cost the same since both reconfigure the composition index
explanation: Lightweight variant switches change only resolved values such as an attribute value, so the composition index is unchanged, making the 'color' set preferable for frequent toggling. The 'lod' set swaps reference paths, which is a heavyweight switch because USD must rebuild parts of its composition index, so any option preferring 'lod' as the lighter or composition-preserving choice inverts which operation is heavyweight. The cost is not the same for both, since value-only changes are far cheaper than structural ones.

stem: An author wants three identical spheres at sibling paths in one scene. They try sublayering the sphere layer three times but only get one sphere. What is the correct mechanism, and why did sublayering fail?
choices: Sublayer the layer under three separate subLayers entries; repeated entries compose as separate copies of the sphere hierarchy
Reference the layer onto three differently named prims; sublayering only overlays specs at the same path, so the spheres just redefined each other
Payload the layer three times onto a single prim; each payload arc in the list brings in a fresh copy of the sphere content
Sublayer three renamed copies of the file; each renamed sublayer grafts its content onto a new sibling path
explanation: Sublayering overlays opinions at the same authored paths with no remapping, so every copy of the sphere layer just redefines the one sphere; referencing the layer onto three differently named prims grafts the content to three distinct paths and yields the siblings. Repeating subLayers entries does not create separate copies, because there is still no way to give them different paths. Stacking payload arcs on a single prim composes them all onto that one prim rather than producing fresh copies. And renaming the sublayered file changes nothing, since sublayers never graft content onto new paths.

stem: An aggregate layer needs to include the same skyscraper asset twice and defer loading a heavy city block. Which composition choices fit each need, given how sublayers, references, and payloads behave?
choices: Reference the skyscraper twice and reference the city block, since references can be loaded and unloaded on demand
Payload the skyscraper twice and sublayer the city block, since sublayers defer loading
Reference the skyscraper twice (sublayering would overwrite it), and payload the city block so it can be loaded on demand
Sublayer the skyscraper twice and reference the city block, since references defer loading
explanation: Adding the same asset twice via sublayers would overwrite it rather than create two copies, so references are required for the duplicated skyscraper, and payloads are like references but can be loaded and unloaded on demand, which is exactly the deferred-loading behavior the city block needs. Options that defer loading via sublayers or references misassign on-demand loading, which belongs to payloads, and references cannot be unloaded on demand the way payloads can.

stem: A reference targets the inner Cube of encapsulated_GOOD.usd as its source prim rather than the World root. The Cube binds a material defined under World. Which statements are correct?
choices: Referencing World instead of Cube would have brought the material along and kept the binding intact
The material is automatically re-pathed under Cube so the binding continues to work
The binding still resolves, because encapsulated assets carry their materials regardless of the source prim chosen
The material binding breaks, because the material under World is outside the scope of a reference whose source is Cube
USD emits a warning that the relationship target refers to a path outside the scope of the reference and ignores the target
explanation: A reference grafts only the targeted source prim's subtree, so targeting Cube excludes the material under World, the binding points outside the reference scope and breaks, and USD warns that the relationship target refers to a path outside the scope of the reference and ignores it. Referencing World instead would have encapsulated the material and preserved the binding. The material is not automatically re-pathed under Cube, and the binding does not still resolve, since choosing an inner source prim drops the out-of-scope material.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Experimenting With Encapsulation

stem: While resolving an attribute under LIVERPS, USD recurses into targeted layer stacks for Inherits, Variants, References, and Payloads. Which statements about how the algorithm recurses are correct?
choices: Recursion evaluates payloads before references inside the targeted layer stack
LIVERPS is applied recursively within each composition context (layer stack)
Specializes ('S') is skipped during recursion into targeted layer stacks and is handled at the end
When recursing into a targeted layer stack, evaluation resumes at the References step instead of starting over from local opinions
Each recursion resolves the targeted stack's local opinions and skips its inherits and variant arcs
explanation: LIVERPS applies recursively within each composition context, and while recursing into the layer stacks targeted by inherits, variants, references, and payloads the Specializes step is skipped and handled specially at the end. Inside a targeted stack, references are still evaluated before payloads, not after. Recursion starts over from the targeted stack's local opinions rather than resuming at the References step. And each recursion re-examines that stack's inherits and variant arcs instead of resolving its local opinions alone.

stem: A developer calls UsdProperty::GetPropertyStack to inspect contributing PropertySpecs but plans to use the returned list to compute the final resolved value. Why is this misuse, especially with layer offsets present?
choices: GetPropertyStack returns the specs in weakest-to-strongest order, so the resolved value must be read from the last entry rather than the first
GetPropertyStack is for debugging only; it omits the time-offsets needed to retrieve correct animated values when layer offsets are present
GetPropertyStack returns only the strongest contributing spec at the given timeCode, which is insufficient when weaker layers carry the animation
GetPropertyStack already applies authored layer offsets to each returned spec, so its values are authoritative for resolution
explanation: GetPropertyStack is documented for debugging and diagnostic use only; it does not carry the time-offsets that must be applied when layer offsets are authored on references, sublayers, or value clips, so computing resolved values from it yields incorrect animated values. The stack lists contributors in strength order for inspection, not as a weakest-first list whose last entry is the answer. It returns every contributing spec, not only the strongest one. And it does not pre-apply authored layer offsets to the returned specs, which is precisely why its contents are not authoritative for resolution.

stem: An override on color authored into weak.usda never appears, because strong.usda already authors color in a stronger sublayer. Without reordering layers, what is the cleanest fix?

snippets.code:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./strong.usda@,
        @./weak.usda@
    ]
)

choices: Re-author the color in weak.usda as timeSamples, since animated values take precedence over a default authored in a stronger layer
Change weak.usda's over to a class specifier so its opinion is inherited over the stronger layer's opinion
Author or redirect the color opinion into strong.usda (or a stronger layer) so it wins value resolution
Author an attribute block for color in weak.usda so the stronger layer's opinion is cleared from composition
explanation: Strength ordering resolves the conflict in favor of strong.usda, so the cleanest fix is to author or redirect the color opinion into strong.usda or another stronger layer so it wins value resolution. Re-authoring the value as timeSamples does not help, because a default in a stronger layer still wins over animated values in weaker layers. The class specifier marks a prim as a source for inherits and does not promote a weaker layer's opinion over a stronger one. And an attribute block authored in the weaker layer cannot clear the stronger layer's opinion, because a block only suppresses opinions weaker than itself.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Composition Arcs and Strength Ordering

stem: A simulation tool deactivates /World/Box to isolate a problem, then traverses the stage with the default Traverse(). What is visited, and is the change recoverable?

snippets.code:
box = stage.GetPrimAtPath("/World/Box")
box.SetActive(False)
for prim in stage.Traverse():
    print(prim.GetPath())

choices: /World/Box itself is excluded but its descendants are still visited, and the change is reversible by setting active back to true
/World/Box and all its descendants are excluded from the traversal, and the change is non-destructive and reversible by reactivating
/World/Box and its descendants are still visited, since the active metadata filters render delegates rather than the default traversal predicate
/World/Box and all its descendants are excluded from the traversal, and the prim's specs are removed so restoring it requires re-authoring
explanation: Deactivating /World/Box is a non-destructive prune: the prim and all of its descendants are excluded from the default traversal, and the change is reversible by reactivating the prim. The diagnosis that only the prim is excluded while its descendants remain visited is wrong because descendants are pruned along with it. The claim that everything is still visited is wrong because the default Traverse() predicate respects the active state; active metadata is not a render-delegate filter. And the claim that the specs are removed so restoring requires re-authoring is wrong because deactivation deletes nothing from the layer.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Active and Inactive Prims

stem: A pipeline authors animated overrides into a USD layer that is composed onto the stage via value clips, but a reference authored inside that clip file is being ignored on the stage. Why?
choices: Opinions introduced through references are weaker than value-clip time samples in LIVERPS, so the clip's samples override the referenced arc
Composition arcs inside a clip are evaluated only at the clip set's first activation time, so the reference drops out for later frames
Value clips contribute attributes through the clip manifest, so a reference inside a clip must instead be declared in the manifest layer to take effect
A UsdStage ignores composition arcs contained in a clip file, so clips can usefully contain only direct local opinions on the attributes they modify
explanation: For performance and scalability, a UsdStage ignores any composition arcs contained in a clip USD file, so value clips can only usefully carry direct local opinions about the attributes they modify; the reference is therefore never composed at all. It is not a LIVERPS strength contest, because the arc is dropped rather than composed and overridden by clip samples. Arcs in clip files are not honored at any frame, so there is no activation-time window in which the reference works. And the clip manifest declares which attributes the clips provide; it is not a site where references from clip layers are honored.

stem: A teammate is unsure how composition relates to value resolution when debugging a slow tool with unexpected resolved values. Which statements from the USD model are correct?
choices: Value resolution rules vary by data type, whereas composition rules vary by composition arc
Composition pre-computes every property's final value, so value resolution is just a lookup
Composition determines final attribute values, so value resolution is unnecessary for attributes
Value resolution is cached per property, while composition is recomputed on every query
Composition is cached at the prim level, while value resolution is not pre-computed
explanation: The cited distinctions are that value resolution rules vary by data type while composition rules vary by composition arc, and that composition is cached at the prim level while value resolution is not pre-computed. The claim that composition pre-computes every property's final value is false because USD deliberately does not pre-compute composed property values, the claim that composition makes value resolution unnecessary is false because composition only finds the sources while value resolution still produces the final value, and the claim that value resolution is cached per property while composition is recomputed every query inverts the actual caching relationship.

stem: A UsdGeomPointInstancer authors only prototypes, protoIndices = [0, 0, 1], and positions, with no ids attribute. What integer id does the third placed instance receive, and from where?

snippets.code:
rel prototypes = [<Prototypes/A>, <Prototypes/B>]
int[] protoIndices = [0, 0, 1]
point3f[] positions = [...]

choices: Id 1, copied from its prototype index value in protoIndices
No id, because ids must be authored explicitly for instances to be addressable
Id 2, inferred from that instance's element index in the protoIndices array
Id 3, a one-based counter assigned in positions order
explanation: ids is optional; when absent, each instance id is inferred from its element index in the protoIndices array, so the third element (index 2) is instance id 2, regardless of its prototype index value.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Point Instancing

stem: For each placed instance, a UsdGeomPointInstancer composes a prototype-root transform, the per-instance scale/orientation/position, and the transform on the PointInstancer prim. Ordered most-local to least-local, which is correct?
choices: Prototype root transform, then scales[i], orientations[i], positions[i], then the PointInstancer prim transform
positions[i], orientations[i], scales[i], then the prototype root transform, then the PointInstancer prim transform
scales[i], orientations[i], positions[i], then the PointInstancer prim transform, then the prototype root transform
The PointInstancer prim transform, then positions[i], orientations[i], scales[i], then the prototype root transform
explanation: Most local is the prototype root transform; then per-instance scales[i], orientations[i], positions[i]; the PointInstancer prim's own transform is applied least locally, letting you move the whole instancer at once.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Point Instancing

stem: A scene uses scenegraph instancing with many instances sharing one prototype. Which refinement edits, authored on the instanceable prims, cause OpenUSD to create a NEW prototype as a result of the edit?
choices: Adding a new ad hoc internal reference to an instanceable prim
Authoring an inherited primvar value on the instanceable prim that a shader reads
Authoring xformOp:translate on the instanceable prim to reposition it
Selecting a different variant on an instanceable prim via a variant set placed there
explanation: Variant-set and ad hoc arc refinements change an instance's composition, so OpenUSD generates a new prototype for the affected instances. Primvar and xformOp refinements only add opinions on the instanceable prim and create no new prototype.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Ad Hoc Arcs Refinement

stem: An identical pose change must be applied to every instance in one group at once while keeping instancing on and authoring a single opinion. The instances share an inherits or specializes arc to a class namespace. Which technique fits?
choices: Deinstancing refinement: set instanceable to false on each prim in the group, then author the pose per copy
Broadcasted refinement: author one opinion on the shared class namespace that the instances' arcs target
Prototype refinement: author the pose on the runtime prototype prim that usdview shows for the group
Hierarchical refinement: author an inherited primvar carrying the pose on each instanceable prim
explanation: Because the instances share an inherits or specializes arc, one opinion authored on the targeted class namespace broadcasts to every instance via LIVERPS while instancing stays on. Deinstancing disables instancing and multiplies the edits, runtime prototype prims are not editable so authoring there yields a dangling opinion, and per-prim primvar refinement requires touching every instanceable prim rather than authoring a single opinion.

stem: A developer sees "/__Prototype_01" in the usdview tree and authors the override below to recolor it. Why does this fail to affect the actual instances?
choices: The override uses constant interpolation, while primvars must use vertex interpolation to reach the instances
The override is composed, but the prototype's opinions are weaker than the instanceable prim's own opinions
The override needs instanceable set to false on the prototype before its opinions can compose onto instances
The override targets a runtime data model that is not editable, leaving a dangling spec unrelated to the real prototype
explanation: The /__Prototype_NN paths shown in usdview are a runtime data model exposed for inspection only; prototypes are not editable, so the over becomes a dangling spec unrelated to the actual prototype. The failure has nothing to do with primvar interpolation, it is not a composition-strength contest between prototype and instance opinions, and instanceable cannot be toggled on a runtime prototype at all.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Introduction to Scenegraph Instance Refinement

stem: An asset references cleanly alone, but referenced into a scene a roof's material:binding is dropped with a warning that the target 'refers to a path outside the scope of the reference.' What principle was violated and how is it fixed?
choices: Default-prim selection: the defaultPrim does not span the material, so set defaultPrim to a common ancestor of geometry and materials
Strength ordering: the binding opinion is weaker than the referencing scene's opinions, so move it into a stronger sublayer
Instancing: the binding targets a prim inside an instance, so set instanceable = false on the building to expose the target
Encapsulation: the material was not a descendant of the entry point; reparent it under the entry point so the reference brings it over
explanation: The warning means the binding's target path falls outside the referenced entry point's scope: only prims beneath the entry point are brought over by a reference, so the material must be reparented under the entry point (encapsulation). defaultPrim selects which prim is referenced but cannot pull in prims outside that subtree. Opinion strength is irrelevant because the target prim simply does not exist in the referencing scene. And instancing is not involved; no instance proxies appear in this scenario, so toggling instanceable changes nothing.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Exercise: Encapsulating Your Asset

stem: In the reference/payload pattern, the interface layer authors an empty class and a variant set above the payload, as below. Why advertise these without authoring any contributing opinions?
choices: Authoring them above the payload registers the asset's composition arcs so the payload can be located and loaded on demand
The class and variant selections compose as stronger opinions that override the payload's contents to force the red selection
Lofting keeps these inexpensive fields discoverable while the payload is unloaded; the class provides an arc target and the variants advertise the selections
They convert the payload arc into a reference arc so the asset's contents compose eagerly during stage population
explanation: Lofting elevates important, inexpensive fields above the payload so they stay discoverable and usable while the payload is unloaded; the lofted class contributes no opinions and just provides a target for the arc, and the lofted variants merely advertise the underlying sets and selections. They are not what registers or locates the payload, which is handled by the payload arc itself. They do not exist to override the payload's contents, because lofted fields contribute no opinions. And nothing about lofting changes the payload into a reference or makes the contents compose eagerly.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Reference/Payload Pattern?

stem: During review a TD finds a leaf Mesh (a gprim) deep in an asset tagged kind = "component". Beyond being unusual, why is this a structural problem for model hierarchy?
choices: The component kind is intended for Xform prims, so Hydra skips the Mesh when populating the render index
A gprim tagged as a component signals a deep model hierarchy, adding composition overhead and losing pruned-traversal gains
kind metadata on a gprim is ignored during composition, so the model boundary silently falls back to the asset root
A component kind on a leaf forces every ancestor to compose as a component as well, inverting the model hierarchy
explanation: A gprim tagged as a component is the explicit sign of a deep model hierarchy, which introduces a small but measurable composition overhead and forfeits the performance gains of pruned traversals. kind is not restricted to Xform prims and Hydra does not skip kind-tagged gprims. kind is read during composition rather than ignored, and there is no fallback of the model boundary to the asset root. And a component tag does not propagate to or convert ancestors, whose kinds are authored independently.

stem: A pipeline architect is validating model-hierarchy rules for an aggregate scene. Which statements are correct?
choices: Subcomponent prims cannot contain other subcomponent prims beneath them in the hierarchy
All ancestors of a component model must have kind set to group or a subkind of group such as assembly
A component model cannot contain another component model as a descendant
Assembly models cannot contain other assembly models beneath them in the hierarchy
explanation: Model hierarchy requires that all ancestors of a component model carry kind group or a subkind of group such as assembly, and that component models, as leaf pruning points, never contain other component models as descendants. The other two rules are false: assemblies may contain other assemblies, and subcomponents may contain other subcomponents, so neither nesting restriction exists for those kinds.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Are Model Kinds?

stem: An asset entry point exposes both a color variant set and a primvar as parameters. With respect to scenegraph instancing of that asset downstream, how do the two parameterization methods differ?
choices: Changing the variant selection generates a new prototype, while authoring the primvar does not
Both always generate a new prototype because they are authored on the entry point
The primvar generates a new prototype, while the variant selection does not
Neither affects prototypes because parameters live on the instanceable prim
explanation: Both are instancing-compatible, but variant selections participate in composition and produce new prototypes for downstream contexts, whereas primvars only add an opinion on the instanceable prim and generate no new prototype, making them lighter.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: What Is Asset Parameterization?

stem: A studio splits an asset into separate geometry and shading layers combined in a layer stack to model parallel user workstreams. Which guidance is correct?
choices: Sequence the workstreams so the shading layer is authored only after the geometry layer is published
Avoid modeling workstreams that grow procedurally over time; layer stacks are not an asset versioning system
Each workstream should author only its unique contributions sparsely rather than overwrite another workstream's work
Merge the workstream layers into a single layer at publish time to avoid per-layer resolution cost
explanation: The recommended guidance is to author each workstream's unique contributions sparsely rather than overwriting other workstreams' opinions, and to keep layer stacks simple by avoiding procedurally growing workstreams, since layer stacks are not an asset versioning system and each layer has a resolve-and-open cost. Sequencing shading strictly after geometry publishes reintroduces the serial bottleneck that parallel workstream layers exist to remove. And merging the layers at publish defeats the nondestructive layered structure; the cost guidance is about avoiding procedural growth, not collapsing layers.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Modeling Workstreams With Layer Stacks

stem: A PointInstancer must hide a subset of instances now but animate them back on at later time codes, while a different, permanent set must be pruned and supports sparse list-editing of which ids it affects. Which properties drive each case?
choices: invisibleIds for the time-animated on/off subset; inactiveIds for the permanent prune, which can be list-edited
protoIndices set to -1 for the hidden subset; the ids array cleared for the permanently pruned set
invisibleIds for the permanent prune, which can be list-edited; inactiveIds for the time-animated subset
inactiveIds for both subsets, with time samples distinguishing the temporary set from the permanent one
explanation: The rule of thumb is invisibleIds for instances that must animate on and off over time and inactiveIds for the permanent prune, and inactiveIds is the one that supports sparse list-editing of ids. The assignment that gives invisibleIds the permanent prune and inactiveIds the animated subset is exactly reversed. protoIndices and ids serve prototype assignment and identification, not hiding or pruning. And inactiveIds alone cannot cover the animated case, because it is not the time-sampled visibility mechanism.

stem: An xformOp:scale has an authored default of (1.5,1.5,1.5) plus time samples {60:(2.5,2.5,2.5),120:(5,5,5)} on a stage whose startTimeCode is 1. Querying GetXformVectors at time code 1 returns which scale, and why?
choices: (2.5,2.5,2.5), because queries before the first sample clamp to the earliest authored time sample
(1,1,1), because the schema fallback applies when no sample exists at the queried time code
(1.5,1.5,1.5), because the authored default value is used before the first time sample
(0.04,0.04,0.04), because values extrapolate linearly backward from the first two samples
explanation: Once time samples are authored they take precedence over the default for timed queries, and a query before the first sample clamps to the earliest authored sample, (2.5,2.5,2.5). The schema fallback applies when nothing at all is authored, the authored default is returned for default-time queries rather than timed ones, and USD holds rather than extrapolates outside the sampled range.

stem: An xformOp:translate has time samples at code 60 = (0,0,2.5) and code 120 = (0,0,5.0), with timeCodesPerSecond = 30. What value resolves at time code 90?
choices: (0,0,3.75), linearly interpolated halfway between the two samples
(0,0,5.0), snapped forward to the nearest authored sample
(0,0,3.0), interpolated using seconds rather than time codes
(0,0,2.5), held from the previous sample until the next sample is reached
explanation: Code 90 is the midpoint of 60 and 120, so USD linearly interpolates: 2.5 + (5.0-2.5)*0.5 = 3.75. Interpolation is on time-code ordinates; timeCodesPerSecond only maps codes to seconds for playback.

source_ref.title: Learn OpenUSD: Time Codes and Time Samples

stem: On a two-quad mesh with 6 points, 2 faces, and faceVertexIndices of length 8, a primvars:displayColor is authored with interpolation = "uniform". How many color values must its array contain?

snippets.code:
int[] faceVertexCounts = [4, 4]
int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 2]
color3f[] primvars:displayColor = [...] (
    interpolation = "uniform"
)

choices: 8, one value per face-vertex index
6, one value per point
2, one value per face
1, a single value for the whole gprim
explanation: Uniform interpolation assigns exactly one value per face. The mesh has two faces (faceVertexCounts = [4,4]), so the array must hold 2 values. Constant would be 1, vertex would be 6.
